items.body: This Mortal Coil, the rotating collective of musicians and vocalists assembled by 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell, released its second studio album, “Filigree & Shadow,” on 22 September 1986 through 4AD. The double LP turns 40 this year. The album gathered 25 tracks, about half of them instrumental, credited to This Mortal Coil but built around a different set of contributors than the project’s 1984 debut. Ivo Watts-Russell and producer John Fryer recorded and mixed “Filigree & Shadow” at Blackwing and Palladium Studios, with arrangements from Simon Raymonde of Cocteau Twins, cellist Martin McCarrick and engineer John Turner, plus violin and viola from Gini Ball. Dead Can Dance percussionist Peter Ulrich and members of Dif Juz, The Wolfgang Press and Colourbox also appeared on the record. Vocalists including Dominic Appleton of Breathless and Alison Limerick sang cover interpretations of songs by Tim Buckley, Gene Clark, Van Morrison, Colin Newman and Talking Heads. “Filigree & Shadow” reached number 53 on the UK Albums Chart and number 2 on the UK Indie Chart, and it streams on Spotify. About This Mortal Coil Ivo Watts-Russell founded 4AD in London in 1980 and built This Mortal Coil a few years later to record music outside the constraints of a fixed band. In 1983 he brought together Cocteau Twins’ Elizabeth Fraser and Robin Guthrie, Cindytalk’s Gordon Sharp and members of Modern English to re-record two Modern English songs as the medley “Sixteen Days/Gathering Dust.” Its B-side, a cover of Tim Buckley’s “Song to the Siren” sung by Fraser and Guthrie alone, entered the UK Singles Chart at number 66 and led Watts-Russell to build a full album around the same idea. That album, “It’ll End in Tears,” followed in 1984 on 4AD. This Mortal Coil never had a fixed lineup. Watts-Russell and engineer John Fryer were its only constant members, and each record drew on a different group of musicians and singers, most pulled from 4AD’s own roster. “Filigree & Shadow” followed in 1986 as the project’s second album, again produced by Watts-Russell and Fryer, with Simon Raymonde, Martin McCarrick and Gini Ball forming its core backing group and Peter Ulrich among the guest musicians. This Mortal Coil closed its studio run with “Blood” in 1991, on which vocalist Caroline Crawley – whose death Side-Line reported in 2016 – was among the featured singers. After the group’s run ended, Watts-Russell continued the same collaborative approach under the name The Hope Blister from 1998, while Fryer went on to produce and engineer widely across the 4AD roster and beyond. “Filigree & Shadow” turns 40 this year, four decades into a project that treated an album as a collaboration rather than the work of a fixed band.

items.body: Some promotion arrives generously late, but with this debut album by the Australian solo project Empty Vessel, I felt it was more than necessary to give it some attention anyway. Tom Wojcicki is an artist unknown to most, who released the album “Ruin Value” in the spring of 2025, an opus consisting of eight tracks. What I hear here defies all imagination: an absolute masterpiece in which the artist blends Industrial, Cinematic, and Ritual elements in a remarkably refined manner. He creates a tormented atmosphere of overwhelming sounds, with percussion effects that reverberate like drones. That overwhelming quality, in particular, is almost indescribable. Rarely have I encountered an artist capable of creating sounds as intense, present, and tormented as those of Empty Vessel. The tracks can be repetitive at times, but because of their sheer intensity, you are truly blown away. Before you know it, you are trapped in a sonic web of terrifying and illusory images. The album is a succession of insane tracks, meaning that you discover one highlight after another. If you are a fan of the genres mentioned above and are not yet familiar with Empty Vessel, I would simply recommend buying this album without listening to it beforehand. An absolute masterpiece, and it will not be easy to follow this up with an equally powerful successor. (Rating:9). Listen to “Scattered Pieces Of Her”: Scattered Pieces Of Her by Empty Vessel About Empty Vessel Empty Vessel is the solo industrial and power electronics project of Australian artist Tom Wojcicki. “Ruin Value” was released on 14 April 2025 through the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen as a hand-numbered CD limited to 200 copies with a 4-page booklet, plus a digital edition, under catalog number DP179CD. The album runs eight tracks, opening with “Scattered Pieces Of Her” and closing with “Zero Fetish”. Empty Vessel has also recorded under the names Droid Sector, Broken Fingers, Glass Barbeque, Aurora Seven and Cockroach Diocese. “Ruin Value” is Empty Vessel’s first release to be reviewed on Side-Line.

items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: " All Art Has Been Contemporary ” This sentence is a neon installation by conceptual artist Maurizio Nannucci located on the roof of the Galleria d'Arte Moderna in Torino, that takes up a similar concept expressed a few decades earlier by Pablo Picasso. Such a fundamental axiom, around which rivers of ink have been spilled, seems to lose its actualization in the late '70s, early '80s, with regard to jazz: this art form is out of sync with the “here and now” and doesn't dialogue with contemporary, ontologically expressed by young generations. Totally deprived of any chance to become aware of free/improv artists, the teens of the time (your humble writer among them) relate to jazz in the same way they approach Dante, Seneca or Milton in highschool or uni: respect, awe, in some cases sincere passion, more often distance. Wright or wrong, a matter of fact. Moreover, those years were destined to write one of the brightest chapters in the Great Book of Music, through amazing groups like Clock DVA, PIL, Joy Division, Talking Heads, Pere Ubu, X, Television, Bad Brains, Wire, just to throw out some names in bulk. Would it have made sense to spend the very little bucks in our pocket on Chet Baker instead of Meat Puppets and Husker Du? C’mon, a no-brainer. This inexhaustible cornucopia of punk/post-punk gems experiences a small, apparently insignificant, intermittence, which leads us, aboard the only ISO-certified Time Machine (the music), to where almost everything happens: New York. Here, while the ruins of CBGB's and Max's Kansas City are still smoking, a patrol of sappers (Contortions, Mars, DNA, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks), pushing far beyond punk, lights up the charges of the “No Wave”, generating a shockwave that transcends the scope of music and involves the most extremist artistic fringes of the East Village and the Lower East Side: poets (Lydia Lunch), writers (Kathy Acker), painters (Basquiat) and filmmakers (Eric Mitchell, Amos Poe) are up for It. Among them, relocated from Minnesota, John Lurie, iconic muse actor from Jim Jarmusch’s early movies, who in his unmissable autobiography, The History of Bones , offers us a snapshot of that sparkling, bohemian milieu: “We were so sure of ourselves, we never doubted anything. We were powerful, intelligent, energetic, confident, self-centered, and incredibly naive. Nothing outside our fourteen-block radius mattered. From Houston to 14th St., from the Bowery to Ave. A, that was the only universe.” John alternates between filmmaking and musical practicing, not on a third-hand Telecaster or on a battered Precision bass, but on alto saxophone: "At 4 p.m. on Main Street in Worcester, Massachusetts, the universe gave me my first saxophone. Nothing special happened, except that a man, driving around with a wheelbarrow, gave me a saxophone. I became like a monk. I slept on the floor, I didn't have a TV, I didn't smoke, I didn't drink, I didn't fuck. I played the saxophone until my fingers bled and I devoured music: Varese, Stravinsky, Mingus, Dolphy, Monk, Bird, Ornette, Hendrix." From there, it was a short step to form a band, and with his brother Evan on keyboards, the rhythm section of Steve Piccolo and Anton Fier (of Feelies “fame”), and the abrasive guitar of DNA’s Arto Lindsay (a very distinctive element of the ensemble), the Lounge Lizards were born, self-described, out of respect for the Masters of the Past, as "fake jazz." The Purists, losers by definition, take the bait and move on, while those with heart and soul stop, listen to and understand the new hybridization of tradition with the metro, iconoclastic, infectious, no-sounds: a sabotage of the “status quo ante” of jazz but, definitively, a Sabotage of Love. None of them graduated from Juilliard (does it matter?), but the Lizards' sound reflects like few others the zeitgeist of Downtown and the mood of those courageous and visionary prime movers who animate it. Their debut album was released in 1981, packaged with Peter Saville's splendid artwork, featuring a black-and-white photo of the musicians on the cover that always reminds us of Jimmy Giuffre's stunning "Free Fall". At the helm, the mighty Teo Macero who infuses the album with the nocturnal atmospheres that made it legendary, sitting the listener at the bar counter of Edward Hopper's "Nighthawks At Diner" or amidst a Raymond Chandler novel. The quick band’s development during the couple of years preceding it is captured on "Live 79-81," a reissue of the 1985 Roir cassette, containing live recordings at Hurrah and CBGB's in New York (June, August 1979), Her Majesty's Theater in London (June 1980), Cleveland Radio (June 1981), and Berlin Jazz Festival (December 1981). It's all there: contractions and swing, dissonances and post-post-bop, Earl Hagan (Harlem Nocturne) and Monk (Epistrophy), boredom and coolness, dark streets and streetlights. Jazz in its pure form. Did Lounge Lizards change the course of events? No. Did they spearhead a new musical stream? No. Did they contribute to ensuring that kids who grew up on punk could relate to jazz in an updated and conscious way? ABSOLUTELY YES. Same as it happened to John Lurie just some years before, then let him have the final words to come full circle: “When I was 17, someone made me listen to John Coltrane and it was as if he was speaking to me in Chinese. But how? Is there music I can't understand? And so I started listening to it all the time.” Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Jason Rigby: tenor and soprano saxophones; Lisa Parrott: alto, soprano, and baritone saxophones; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Cameron Brown: bass; Tony Jefferson: drums. Bassist and composer Cameron Brown has always felt comfortable in both traditional and avant-garde settings, and was an important element in the rhythm sections behind Archie Shepp, Don Pullen, George Adams, George Russell, Dewey Redman, and Don Cherry. Here, he leads a chordless quintet, paying tribute to Cherry as well as his mentor Dannie Richmond, best known for his extensive work with the one-and-only bassist, composer, and bandleader Charles Mingus. This ensemble started as a quartet featuring saxophonist Jason Rigby, trumpeter Russ Johnson, and drummer Tony Jefferson. Saxophonist Lisa Parrott joins them here for a dense, unfiltered session recorded live in concert in 2011. Raw and dense, it often sounds like a jam. The uptempo “ Sheila, It’s You! ”—written for the late jazz vocalist Sheila Jordan—has the three-horn frontline blowing with hard-bop intensity over the hard-charging swing provided by the rhythm section. They alternate solos before intersecting their searing lines with purpose. Conversely, “ Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie ” is a 3/4 ballad gently propelled by brushes. “ Baby Suite ” is a through-composed response to Cherry’s “cocktail suite” concept. Brown’s three-minute bass monologue—featuring double-stops and thoughtful melodic development—right after the contrapuntal theme leads into faster bass circularity, with Jefferson free to embellish while the horns float above. A spontaneous avant-garde freedom reminiscent of Mingus’ excursions can be felt in the coda that precedes the theme. “ Cocktail Suite ”, which clocks in at 21 minutes and includes Cherry’s “ Remembrance ” and “ OC/DC ”, Jobim’s “ Portrait in Black and White ”, and Redman’s “ Mushi Mushi ”, features some awkward passages and elongated solos with the horns left to roam freely. Incessant walking lines populate the recording, creating an inescapable sense of anticipation. Brown’s “ Rylie’s Bounce ” blooms with a bass solo at the outset and explosive drumming by Jefferson, who throws in some barbed percussive sounds on Richmond’s “ Soft Seas ”, an amusing calypso dance served with humor and panache. Parrott causes some frisson on baritone, while Rigby explores the opposite end of the spectrum on soprano. This piece is put together much more effectively, with a keen sense of time and a divergence from conventional swing. With the interplay controlled at all times and the recording sounding like a classic, Remembrance sometimes rings a bit meandering, yet never disjointed. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Baby Suite ► 03 - Soft Seas ► 07 - Cocktail Suite

items.body:
STARGLOW are looking back at where it all began with their new single, 'WISHES'. Released on 22 September, the Japanese pop single serves as an answer song to 'PIECES', the track performed by the finalists of BMSG's THE LAST PIECE during the audition programme's final stage.

While 'PIECES' captured the hopes and uncertainty surrounding the finalists at the time, 'WISHES' revisits those feelings one year later. Now together as STARGLOW, the five members reflect on the memories and connections they have made since then while looking towards their next chapter.

The single also sees all five members taking part in its writing and composition. They are credited alongside Bad Milk, PALMR, and SKY-HI — the same creative team behind 'PIECES'. PALMR handled the arrangement, while SKY-HI and PALMR produced the track.

'WISHES' arrives as STARGLOW mark their first pre-debut anniversary. The group will commemorate the occasion with a livestream at 9 PM JST on 22 September, featuring a live vocal performance and what has been teased as a "major announcement" about their next steps. The official lyric video for 'WISHES' will premiere immediately after at 9:30 PM JST.

The release also comes ahead of STARGLOW's debut album, Aurora, due out on 18 November. The 14-track record will bring together songs from across the group's journey so far, including 'Moonchaser', 'Drivin' My Life', and 'WISHES', alongside five additional new tracks.

From the questions that surrounded 'PIECES' to the memories behind 'WISHES', STARGLOW have turned the two songs into bookends for their first chapter together — one capturing where their journey began, and the other answering it a year later.

items.body:
Apple has opened the doors to a new home for live music in London.

Announced on 21 September, Apple Music Hall is a new 600-capacity live music venue located inside the historic Battersea Power Station. Designed for intimate performances with arena-level production capabilities, the space will host one-off shows that can also be livestreamed to fans around the world.

The venue marks Apple's latest investment in bringing artists and audiences together, following a history of music initiatives that includes the iPod, iTunes, the long-running iTunes Music Festival, and Apple Music.

“Apple’s deep love for music dates all the way back to the very beginning, from the launch of the iPod to the long-running iTunes Music Festival to the debut of Apple Music,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple's Vice President of Apple Music and International Content.

“Today, with the opening of Apple Music Hall, we are once again taking an unprecedented step further in our commitment to artists and fans by supporting live music in ways only Apple can do.”

An intimate venue with arena-scale production

Taking its visual cues from Battersea Power Station itself, Apple Music Hall incorporates heritage brickwork, fluted arches, and bronze balconies inspired by the building's historic oriel windows. A large glass wall also looks out towards the concourse and River Thames.

At the heart of the venue is a 38-foot-wide stage that can be reconfigured depending on the performance. Artists can opt for a traditional front-facing setup or create more immersive, in-the-round experiences.

The 600-person capacity keeps audiences close to the action, but behind that intimate setup is infrastructure designed to accommodate productions on a much bigger scale.

A 48-speaker spatial sound system surrounds the audience, allowing performances created for spatial audio to be experienced immersively throughout the venue.

Apple Music Hall is also built as a recording and broadcast facility. Two dedicated studios can capture shows as multitrack recordings and mix them in Spatial Audio, either live or after the performance.

For video, the venue is hardwired to support 16 or more cameras connected to a purpose-built broadcast control room. Its infrastructure can also accommodate iPhone video capture alongside traditional broadcast cameras.

In practical terms, an artist could play a single intimate show and come away with a finished Spatial Audio recording, broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video of the performance.

Apple Music Hall performances will stream globally

While Apple Music Hall itself is in London, its shows aren't intended to stay within its 600-person walls.

Apple said performances from the venue will also be livestreamed globally, giving fans outside London a chance to watch its one-off concerts remotely.

“At Apple Music, we care deeply about music, the artists who make it, and their life stories,” said Zane Lowe, Apple Music's Global Creative Director and lead anchor for Apple Music 1.

“We’re always looking for new opportunities to connect the artists and the fans because we are fans. What better way to celebrate this relationship than a new music venue where we get to experience amazing music in an amazing space and share it with the world.”

Lowe added: “Great music and memories will be made at Apple Music Hall.”

Apple Music Radio gets a new London home

Apple's expansion at Battersea also includes a new base for Apple Music Radio.

All of Apple Music Radio's London-based hosts and programmes will now broadcast live from new studios inside Battersea Power Station.

The studios will continue to host the interviews, artist specials, global premieres, and surprise performances that form part of Apple Music Radio's programming. The service broadcasts around the clock and is available to listeners worldwide for free.

The opening brings Apple's live performance, recording, broadcasting, and radio operations together at Battersea, with Apple Music Hall giving artists a space where a single performance can reach both the audience in the room and listeners and viewers around the world.

Details on upcoming Apple Music Hall performances and ticket access are available via Apple Music Hall's official channels.

items.body:
BLACKPINK star LISA has teamed up with PlayStation to launch the LISA x PlayStation collection on 30 October, featuring a limited-edition DualSense wireless controller designed in collaboration with the Thai rapper and singer.

Decked out in a Chroma Pearl colourway, the DualSense wireless controller – LISA Limited Edition features LISA's signature bangs and eyes across its touch pad, alongside stars and bold "LL" lettering.

"Gaming is something I do whenever I have time to relax, so getting to create this collection with PlayStation was very exciting," shared LISA. "I had a lot of fun adding in little details that I knew my fans would notice, and I wanted the fans to have something they can connect with."

The collaboration will also extend to a merchandise collection in the U.S., including apparel, hats, tote bags, keychains, stickers, and a DualSense controller carrying case. Select pieces will be available for pre-order via PlayStation from 2 October, while additional merchandise will arrive on LISA's official Amazon store on 23 October.

The drop coincides with another release from LISA — her new EP, Press Play, which is also slated to arrive on 23 October.

The controller will be released globally in limited quantities for US$84.99 / ¥12,480 / €84.99 / £74.99, with pre-orders opening on 2 October at 10 AM local time, while stocks last.

In the U.S., fans can pre-order the DualSense wireless controller – LISA Limited Edition and select pieces from the LISA x PlayStation merchandise collection from 10 AM ET on 2 October via direct.playstation.com. The items will launch on 30 October.

Fans in the U.K., France, Germany, Austria, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg can pre-order the limited-edition controller from 10 AM local time on 2 October via playstation.com/store/hardware. Quantities will be limited, with the controller launching on 30 October.

The controller will also be available through participating retailers globally from 30 October, subject to availability.

items.body:
JISOO has completed her four-part transformation for self-portrait’s latest fashion campaign.

The BLACKPINK member has unveiled the final three characters from Portraits of a Screen Star, following the campaign’s opening chapter, The Enigma, earlier this month.

Shot in Seoul by Oliver Hadlee Pearch, the campaign takes the form of a series of imagined audition tapes, with JISOO portraying four cinematic personas through different performances and looks.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by self-portrait (@mrselfportrait)

Following The Enigma came The Muse, an elegant, magnetic and misunderstood character dressed in a pale pink satin slip dress with feather trim.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by self-portrait (@mrselfportrait)

JISOO then stepped into The Ingénue, a candy-coloured, dreamy and observant persona. For the third look, she wore a grey flower wool jumper paired with a green satin bow mini skirt and cream satin pink floral beaded oval clutch.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by self-portrait (@mrselfportrait)

Rounding out the series is The Optimist. Described as unhurried, serene and gently certain, the final character sees JISOO wearing a brown off-shoulder collar top, black capri knit leggings and pearl flower beaded cluster earrings.

With The Optimist joining The Enigma, The Muse and The Ingénue, all four characters from Portraits of a Screen Star have now been revealed.

Speaking about the campaign, JISOO shared how each wardrobe helped her find the nuances of her different performances.

“The evolution of the character's wardrobe was how I found the nuance in each performance and it was a real collaboration with Han and I on finding the subtlety in each role I was going to be playing,” she said.

“I have worn self-portrait for many years, and the pieces make me feel like I can do anything — this time, they let me dream that I could be anyone.”

items.body:
After four years of taking After Hours Til Dawn around the world, The Weeknd has begun its final chapter in Asia.

The Canadian artist kicked off the tour's first-ever Asian leg with back-to-back shows at Tokyo's Belluna Dome on 19 and 20 September, marking his first return to Japan in seven years. The dates opened a 17-show run that will travel through Jakarta, Singapore, Seoul, Bangkok, Hong Kong, and Kuala Lumpur.

And for the opening night, The Weeknd had a surprise made especially for Japan.

Yoko Takahashi joined him onstage for a special rendition of 'A Cruel Angel’s Thesis', the iconic opening theme from Neon Genesis Evangelion. The pair also debuted a new song together, accompanied by visuals from Yoko Taro that incorporated imagery from NieR:Automata and Neon Genesis Evangelion.

Across the two-hour set, The Weeknd revisited different corners of his catalogue with 'Popular', 'One of the Girls', 'Less Than Zero', 'Kiss Land', and 'Blinding Lights'. 'Out of Time' also featured Tomoko Aran, while Japanese hip-hop duo Creepy Nuts and DJ ¥ØU$UK€ ¥UK1MAT$U joined the opening shows as special guests.

The Japanese influence extended far beyond the music. Towering over the stage was a roughly 12-metre-tall gold sculpture by Hajime Sorayama, hand-carved by craftsmen in Toyama and fitted with lasers in its eyes and smoke effects in its palms. The massive centrepiece is also the largest commissioned fine artwork incorporated into a live concert production.

Japanese contemporary artist Tetsuya Nakamura created masks worn by The Weeknd onstage, while Yohji Yamamoto POUR HOMME designed special looks for the tour. The production's combination of music, fashion, visual art, and Japanese pop culture gave the opening dates an identity specific to the tour's long-awaited arrival in Asia.

After Belluna Dome, The Weeknd heads across Asia before bringing After Hours Til Dawn to its final dates at Kuala Lumpur's TM Stadium Nasional on 4 and 5 November.

items.body: A saxophonist by nature, Calum Builder couldn’t help but think of the brass instrument while salvaging old church organ pipes in Northern Denmark, regarding the organ as “another aerophone working with a different kind of breath.” Honoring the prophecy of his surname, he built a reconstructed organ portable enough to take on tour. Enlisting the aid of vocalists Johanna Sulkunen and Zola Mennenöh, he combines these sounds with fragment of psalms, creating a sound that is part palimpsest, part excavation. The opening tracks are each a quarter-hour in length, allowing the listener to dive deep into the waters of divinity. “Where Can I Go” takes its lead from Psalm 139 and pairs beautifully with Andrzej Pietrewicz & Haiyue Zhu’s #10 from last year. At first there are only forlorn taps and tones, a hint of flute, a sense of desolation: hot winds blowing across even hotter sand. The darker tones come across as howls: the keening cry of the djinn. After five minutes, the harmonies emerge like an oasis, beginning the thought (“Where can I go?”) without revealing the full passage. As the vocalists sing louder and shift intonation, their repetitions become prayers. The reconstructed organ recedes, clearing space for their words to waft to the heavens. A vocal loop rides atop an organ drone, then breaks free, growing faster and more insistent. Listeners unfamiliar with the psalm may miss the underlying comfort in the unspoken words that follow, communicated only through the breath of the pipes until the closing, consoling minute. The opening timbre of “Surely” is like that of a train horn, recalling the steam engines of earlier times. One begins to muse on the similarities between instruments. Apart from being a punchline in the movie “Airplane!”, the word surely is found dozens of times in Scripture and most famously in the 23rd Psalm. Builder chooses the lesser known Psalm 139:11-12, NIV: If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me and the light become night around me,” even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day, for darkness is as light to you. Behind the gorgeous vocals, a drone of darkness rises like a shroud, eclipsing but not eliminating the words. Again – as in the psalm – the overlying tone is foreboding, like an accumulated mass of daily troubles, but the underlying message is that God is still present, just as the notes remain in the pipes even after they have been removed from the church organ. The thin tendrils of sound that close the piece are like the last vestiges of night retreating from the day as the piece topples. without pause into “Is As Light.” This final movement contains some of the highest vocal notes and lowest organ notes, a contrast that underlines the theme. The album title quotes the Latin Eadem mutata resurgo, which relates not only to the logarithmic spiral, but to the nature of the soul. As famous Swiss mathematician Jakob Bernoulli writes, “The logarithmic spiral may be used as a symbol either of fortitude and consistency in adversity, or of the human body, which after all these changes, even after death, will be restored to its exact and perfect self.” Calum Builder’s album may refer more to the first, but ultimately points the way to the second. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Magic Hour is both accessible and deeply experimental with its mutant ambient approach. The sonic palette employs clicks and clacks, echoes, mechanical whirs, lost terrestrial train whistles, melodic forms, shattering forms, and human murmurs, sometimes slowing or speeding up local fields to gain an emotional edge. Continuous processes of deconstruction and reconstruction Magic Hour by FeLid   Time is not a reliable empirical concept, Magic Hour combines improvisational and accidental guitar sounds, lyrical ambient drones, and high-definition sound editing. Magic Hour is both accessible and deeply experimental with its mutant ambient approach. The sonic palette employs clicks and clacks, echoes, mechanical whirs, lost terrestrial train whistles, melodic forms, shattering forms, and human murmurs, sometimes slowing or speeding up local fields to gain an emotional edge. Sharp, jarring cuts where one familiar sound instantly morphs into a new field. Drawing on all available sonic materials—including instrumental sounds, electronics, fragments of recorded audio, and environmental sounds—FeLid creates tracks and improvisational live performances through continuous processes of deconstruction and reconstruction. So many examples. Sounds with backwards envelopes, where the natural decay of a noise happens before its sharp impact. Freezing a specific moment or target in complete temporal suspension. Magic Hour is the second album by Tokyo-based artist FeLid, who combines improvisational and accidental guitar sounds, lyrical ambient drones, and high-definition sound editing. His practice is designed as a shared exploration of the relationship between sound and space, inviting audiences to experience and discover these connections together in real time. FeLid is the solo project of Kazutoshi Eguchi. He is known as a member of the post-hardcore band the north end and as a co-organizer of the festival platform MIMINOIMI. A collage of percussion instruments :: I am imagining dry mountain water, such as found in a Japanese rock garden. “Karesansui in the air #2” (5:14) opens into a collage of percussion instruments, wooden objects being tapped or struck, a curiously nourishing soup of casual fast easy flowing sounds. Here the passage of time is an objective measure. “Hello, World” (3:37) might be a welcome transparent soup of small items. Behind everything there is steamy condensation dripping and falling into a puddle on the ground, forming clusters with little gaps. Next the beat is bubbling and walking by itself, the feeling brings little scenes that open and close, and return, “Magic hour (disco)” (4:37). The ticking of the clock machinery is dark and hidden things are happening all around. The next thing I remember, I awakened in an “Environmental Mood” (3:13). We are washing stuff in the cave, bumping and scrubbing, spilling water and tossing things around, the scrubbing is the beat. Time to go to work. “Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower? “Yuudachi Dub #2” (2:44) brings a different lathe creature here, chattering away faster, sometimes speeding like a demon, with a jittery beat, moving really quickly along, faces appear flattened in the direction they are traveling, the clock on board stretches. Our spaceship appears to move very slowly. “”Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower?” ~Robin B. James Hold on, this next track is less than a minute in duration, “Akirame Mo Kanzin” (0:58). Metal stuff and small percussion instruments are being tapped, played backwards and forwards, very busy until the end, that occurs in an apparently irreversible succession from the past, through the present, and into the future. Now I am floating in the dark waters, “Harmonics Dub” (1:51), barely bobbing on the surface. I love the sound of guitar harmonics, textures made by energizing the strings, a mandolin being dusted off, searching for something. This turns out to lead into a haunted house, where we can play ping pong, “Sense of Gradation” (5:56) blends drone like textures with the steady ping pong tok tok tok sounds, a sound collage of real-world noises that have been warped, looped, and recontextualized into an abstract sonic experience, never busy, accenting the constant drone​ of imaginary wire strings being provoked, while the ping pong activities continue, proving the ability to use magic related to time. FeLid is also a member of MIMINOIMI, an organizing collective dedicated to exploring ambient and experimental music from multiple perspectives, and is involved in the planning and production of the urban festival Ambient / Week. Magic Hour is available on ato.archives. [Bandcamp] Magic Hour by FeLidThe post FeLid :: Magic Hour (ato.archives) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Finnforest — A Charming Entrance Salis was a band from Sardinia named for the two Salis brothers, Antonio and Francesco. They wouldrelease three albums in the 1970s and be yet another inhabitant of that deep RPI back bench. Farbeyond the many well-known classic Italian pop/rock bands getting respect and attention on thesurface, there were so many other bands who never made the front bench. Even many prog fans whoembrace the existence of RPI may not have heard of a band like Salis. And yet, so many of theseobscure groups have work that is worthy of attention even if it is not the full-blown progressiverock that would follow later in the decade.While most people will point to their "proggiest" third album, it is the this debut that is of mostinterest to me. It joins a crucial group of Italian proto-RPI bands who set the stage for what wascoming just around the bend. This group of bands ranges from Italian pop to blues rock to psychrock, all pushing the barriers of their own zone while releasing work that was not quite fullyformed progressive rock. Some are just okay and some are quite exciting. This is one of the betterones in my view. While you have the short song format and bluesy-jazzy psych rock variations, theirsecret weapon is their passion and an amazing feel for memorable little motifs that are not alwayspredictable. They begin to seep into your head after just a couple spins, and I think it may besttheir other two releases that get most of the attention. This first Salis album is a must for RPIfans who like stuff like Fabio Celi, Il Mucchio, and Equipe 84. Sometimes the special sauce is justyouth.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The most atypical album of David Byrne's career is also his darkest, a record where he returned to experimentation, not with world music or electronica as he had at other times, but with rock in a way he hadn't since the early days of Talking Heads. It was 1994, the era of indie and alternative rock; much had changed since 1992, the year of his previous studio album. That shift may well have influenced the group of musicians he assembled, a lineup that was anything but accidental, featuring Arto Lindsay on guitar (previously with the Lounge Lizards, John Zorn, and Marc Ribot), John Medeski on organ, Bill Ware on vibraphone (formerly of The Jazz Passengers and Groove Collective), and Bebel Gilberto, the daughter of Jo�o Gilberto."A Long Time Ago" begins to unfurl a descending, subtle mist amidst soft layers of guitar, synthesizers, and percussion, while the vocals, initially a mere whisper with a dreamlike, psychedelic quality, gradually begin to reveal their full power. Then, a sonic explosion, driven by distorted guitars and a prominent bassline, sweeps through everything in "Angels." Lyrics full of defiance and poetry, philosophical, too, delivered with deep emotion and vocal power; that vocal timbre also always held a touch of Adrian Belew, at least in its more melodic sense. And when he hit those high notes, leaving just the strumming guitar, accompanied by the bass and his voice declaring he was ready, it was a magnificent moment. It opened up from within like an explosion of light, unlike anything seen before in his career, quite the paradox for his darkest album."Crash" bursts in with a syncopated rhythm, like shattering glass; it is one of those albums where each track is sonically conceived in relation to the one preceding it, adding extra value. A dissonant guitar, paired with unconventional drumming, lends a unique touch, evoking a walk through ruins. It is as if the Smashing Pumpkins and Soundgarden were attempting a funk sound; that is how unusual the blend is, yet it succeeds brilliantly, driven by that deliberately fractured rhythm... all held together by the glue of the vocals."A Self-Made Man" has a hypnotic rhythm and a melody that gradually reveals itself to be magical and spellbinding, as he sings: "Well, I'll trade you my potential, mental illness for your bad teeth. And now we have a black market. A black market for designer genes. They've taken everything from you: the way you walk, the way you smile, the sound of your voice. I don't even know who you are. Who are you now? I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to give) I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to lose)"That is how groundbreaking this album was, and not just musically; although I like several of his solo albums, this one holds a very special place."Back In The Box" sounds modern; the guitars, featuring Arto Lindsay on the more experimental side and David Byrne on the funk side, combined with the bass and the melody in David's phrasing, create a sort of deconstructed Krautrock, albeit heavily distorted, as is the case across most of the album. The familiar Latin rhythms take on a mysterious air here, as evidenced by "Sad Song", while the energy never flags; John Medeski contributes a "gritted-teeth" rhythmic intensity that maintains its drive regardless of genre shifts."Nothing At All" reveals more of Byrne's true essence: he lays his voice bare, stretching notes to their limit amidst dissonant guitar rhythms and a sense of mystery that offers no clues as to his intentions. Only at the very end does he begin to unravel the harmonic thread, a move clearly planned from the start, concluding with instrumental codas driven by heavy cymbal work alongside distorted guitar and organ."My Love Is You" opens with bossa nova-style acoustic guitar notes, then shifts into a stark contrast to what came before, courtesy of Bill Ware. "Lilies Of The Valley" returns to playful, experimental rhythms, driven by a powerful bass and drum foundation, packed with Groove, that builds in intensity while the funk guitar seems to lock in perfectly with David. The finale is a marvelous duet between Todd Turkisher's drums and Bill Ware's vibraphone."You & Eye" keeps the syncopated funk going, with David playing the clavinet, and features a very delicate chorus that contrasts with the melody's frenetic rhythm. He hadn't lost that knack for composing songs that strike a direct chord, quite the opposite; here, there are echoes of African music in the style of Salif Keita. With Dolette McDonald on backing vocals, the same one who had worked with Sting, Stevie Winwood, and many others."Strange Ritual" is one of the key tracks, where that opening mist returns, dark and dangerous, like Naked City, while the lyrics go: "A man sits in a field, contemplating his crops. Scenes that disgust me, I see myself, I felt awe, I felt disgust, I felt bliss, I felt lust, It is not unusual, I saw people in a remote village, proudly sporting their digital watches. I saw a young Indonesian woman, possessed by the spirit of the Ninja Turtles. I saw palatial mansions with decaying decor and human furniture. I saw a legislature of women being courted by corporate lobbyists. A town whose own inhabitants do not even remember its name. We have a strange ritual. We keep it to ourselves. We are lost in love"There is a restrained violence, and gradually, in the vein of King Crimson's "Indiscipline", a section marked by calm and camouflaged rage, by a lurking violence, erupts; the vocals shift in tandem with the intensity of the music and the musicality of the words. From the mist emerges a nightmare where playing the lead role isn't frightening, because we are in control. We will never hear a more rock-oriented, fully committed David Byrne; it brings to mind King Crimson's improvisations on Starless and Bible Black. It is almost on that level."Buck Naked" is essentially just the guitar, John Medeski's organ, and David's vocals, with him giving it his all, whether in moments of presence or absence. It plays with the contrasts between calm and rage seen in his Psycho Killer era. Yet there is no nostalgia here; he breaks away from the past to launch a new phase, unafraid to keep experimenting and embracing new influences, much as he would later do with the Balanescu Quartet on 1997's Feelings. However, nowhere else is there such a sincere, honest, and unadorned outpouring of the heart as on this album, which, like the other side of a mirror, features his surname spelled in reverse.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Once again fabulously illustrated by Annette Appleton in a captivating pictorial style?part na�ve, part naturalistic, and slightly dreamlike?*Estanyo Nord* is the last album by the English duo The Light Afternoon, aka Steve Newland, the ultra-perfectionist multi-instrumentalist, and Annette Appleton, the singer-illustrator with a shy, fairy-like voice. To illustrate the cover of *Estanyo Nord* and the inside poster, Annette was determined to depict the Panorama house and its surroundings as a veritable Garden of Eden, with a profusion of very real animals?mostly birds and cats, but also dogs and a gecko?in a visionary and imaginative style that makes this miraculous bestiary seem surreal and symbolic.The album tells the story of this exotic miniature Walden, a little lost paradise, just a stone's throw from the road and a short walk from the sea, and of its inhabitants? whether human (Ana Cirema and all the other souls of the household) or non-human?mostly cats ("Our Time In The Tin North")?who thrived in Panorama under a dark velvet sky streaked with shooting stars. Conceptually and structurally, *Estanyo Nord* is divided into two distinct parts ("Part One: Anacirema," "Part Two: Estanyo Nord"), like the two sides of a vinyl record, each consisting of four tracks, 4 or 5 minutes per track, for a total running time of 38 minutes?thus respecting the spirit and constraints of vinyl records from their heyday. All of this is significant because *Estanyo Nord* draws heavily on the past?from nostalgic memories of Steve and Annette's personal histories to the musical past of everyone who lived through the '80s to the fullest, in a way that was deceptively carefree yet truly full of hope, filled with both certainties and doubts. " "I don't know what makes me happy, I just know what makes me sad, I do my best to remember all the things that make me glad" ("All Of These Things," luminous memories of Malta, France, and Spain) "Musically, Estanyo Nord is very different from our previous album because Steve didn't want to make *The History of Mr. Puffin Man?The Sequel*" (dixit Annette). One couldn't put it better. As dynamic and assertive as the previous album was languid, gentle, and undulating, *Estanyo Nord* has categorically moved away from the dark symphonic prog of La Renaissance or Dead Can Dance, with the instrumental sounds and rhythmic programming here very clearly oriented toward synth-pop. But both albums share the same melancholy and a highly cinematic approach to music, with subtle touches of modulation and tense minor chords. This is particularly evident from the very start of "Wide Open Highway Road Movie," with its *Midnight Express*-like atmosphere, its sharp guitar chords and solos set against highway rhythms, and its synths so distinctly '80s that you can almost hear that faint vintage hiss that followed each synth note, following the strange hum of the electric current that had set them vibrating. With a slower sequenced tempo, "The Girl from Panorama" is more reminiscent of Kraftwerk or the early Human League. Meanwhile, the more high-energy "Anacirema" and "Estanyo Nord"?true hit potential?blend new wave rock and dance music much as New Order did a few years ago. Those who enjoyed the symphonic harmonies of *The History Of Mr Puffin Man* might prefer "The Paradero" and "All of These Things," with their delicate, haunting melodies, piano arpeggios, mysterious or commanding synths, subtle vocal arrangements, and that guitar that reminds me of Pulsar's *Gorlitz* (1989) in a slightly decadent, fin-de-si�cle (20th-century) atmosphere that evokes Bowie's legendary and unconventional *Low*. This European atmosphere is present with even more tenderness and romanticism on the slow "Watching the Perseids," a small, classically influenced pocket symphony. "Our Time in the Tin North" is closer to the atmospheric post-prog of Soup or North Atlantic Oscillation or the dreamy electronica of Tangerine Dream's latest albums, which should appeal to most of us. But regardless of our musical preferences and how open-minded we are in this regard, it would be a shame to miss this precious opportunity to own such an artistic work?one that is as valuable for its visual presentation as for its musical content. At first glance, it may seem relatively far removed from the usual canons of progressive rock, but ultimately, it is as universal as beauty itself.

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4 .5 stars.It is difficult to add any more eloquent words than Fernando has already said. It took me more than a few plays to grasp this work. That is a good thing, all too often find something immediately likeable, then wonder why I liked it a week later I hate it. However, this album has longevity, as I also believe the band has.This is a band that will stay the course, with the brilliant, and classically trained Nat Bergrin at the helm, this music is a true delight for all fans of the more progressive/experimental side of rock.Whilst I think it's fair to say that most of us love retro-sounding bands, you will only get glimpses of that from this most excellent and progressive of albums.When I first played disc, I thought "Oh wow!" a garage rock band playing very complex prog rock, which I do still stand by in some ways. But the technicality of all the players involved pushes it well beyond a garage rock band in any conventional sense. I love that they are a not a paint by numbers neo rock band. This is a band pushing musical boundaries, and I love the direction that they are taking. I love their earlier album 'Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun', but this album enters a whole new realm. This is an album well worth checking out, if your penchant is for progressive Jazz, Classical, black metal... etc. etc....In fact, if you really love the progression of progressive rock music, then this is not a band to be missed.

I gave it a three stars review.Lullabies for the Marooned clocks in at three quarters of an hour.The music here is art-rock.The band, I mean duo, has retreated from the more rocking soundscape on their debut album into amuch more intimate, softly spoken and refined soundscape on their new album, the follow-up album.Early Genesis, Procol Harum, Sylvan, Talk Talk and Peter Hammill are good references here. There areeven some Steve Hogarth era Marillion lurking around in their music too. There is a blend of acoustic and electric instruments here, including guitars. The strings is addinga lot of colours and are complementing the great vocals.This is an album where a piece of music crosses over to becoming an artwork. The result is a great album and one of this year's better albums from Norway, the new powerhouse inart-rock and prog rock. 4 stars

items.body: Review by alainPP — Uncompromising art rock for a fresh sound, minimalist and captivating alternative electro-prog."My Blistering Mind" boasts a distinctive sound, phrased vocals, and electronic, synth-heavy orchestration reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. A final mantra-like repetition of the gentle chorus shifts between pop, cold wave, and Bowie-esque dance-pop-rock, all set to poignant lyrics about mental fragility. "The Mandatory Prize" features a synthetic riff on electric piano, a long, melancholic, and pervasive melody set to lyrics by Dick, with a sound reminiscent of Steve Wilson. Malcolm's voice is ever-present, pale, cold, and robotic, mirroring the synth pads in a new prog style. But that riff is truly gut-wrenching. "Never Really Felt Like Home," with its ambient, hypnotic, and contemplative intro, and Kathryn's deep flute, is a symbol of tranquility. The piccolo allows for a drift into a cinematic-melancholic space where the low guitar solo amplifies this beatific, solemn instrumental. "Smile, Smile, Smile," already seen on the EP, has a haunting metronomic sound on the vibrating bass, the keyboard unfolding, flirting with Esth�sie, the addictive vocals leading to saturation. An electronic Wilson, like his side project No-Man. A stressful, redundant finale leading to musical madness through its endless repetition, the lyrics cruelly explaining this moment of schizoid disarray. "Intermission," as its name suggests, is an instrumental on bass and drums with a jazzy piano, a way of dreaming about the evolution of jazz today. The ensuing Mellotron chills the ears before the colorful piano nods to the works of Joe Jackson."Parallel Lives," with its hushed vocals and contemplative ballad-like feel, sees Kathryn's guitar work on the chorus amplify its solemnity. The effective rhythmic foundation drives this lament, reminiscent of Springsteen's "Streets of Philadelphia." The eponymous track plunges into the depths of Wavy's pop. "Eversion," one of the longer pieces, meanders with lyrics reminiscent of Kate Bush, its orchestration blending neoclassical, synth, and electronic elements, inspired by Steve Wilson. A piano and synth interlude precedes the electric return and Malcolm's vocals, sly, dark, and haughty. The guitar solo brightens the ear, and the sound returns with hypnotic, syncopated percussion, amplifying the progressive, schizophrenic feel. "Pretty Blue Fox" opens with a modern, electro-synth feel, reminiscent of Tangerine Dream in the 70s. It's a blend of electro and prog, with a satisfying mid-section, scraping away at the repetitive sounds of Philip Glass for a restrained, immersive, orgasmic finale ? pure bliss. "Just Another Thing" returns to new prog rock with its piercing, guttural vocals; you'll want to try these breathless vocalizations yourself. There's a hint of Bowie, a sound reminiscent of Simple Minds, a dynamic track with a neo-Marillion-esque keyboard solo, recounting Malcolm's retinal mishaps. "Dropping The Mask" is another instrumental with an electrified, upbeat tempo and bouncy keyboard, a nod to Tangerine Dream in the 80s ? groovy, energetic, and catchy. "Just Hold On (Pts 1 & 2)" opens with a religious, elegiac intro, the soaring choir drifting into hyperspace?a fitting way to escape this groundbreaking album. A striking mix of languid atmosphere and archaic feel, thanks to a guitar emerging from a cloud of Olympus, the solo spreading to the heavens. Malcolm finally appears on this melting synth, the drums merely controlling the rhythm. A solemn ambiance is created by the double bass, the deep vocals, the ephemeral piano, and the final, melancholic guitar outro, a meditative and hopeful finale. A truly beautiful and contemplative ending. "My Blistering Mind," in a shorter, perhaps faster version, and "The Mandatory Prize" are released as radio edits, destined for the airwaves of a better world.HATS OFF GENTLEMEN IT'S ADEQUATE blends vocal and purely instrumental tracks, delivering electronic art-rock with contemporary classical touches. A modern progressive rock sound for the new millennium. (4.5)

items.body: Review by alainPP — NORTH SEA ECHOES, nothing new except for extending their first offering: heavier, more melancholic, more pervasive."A Time of Innocence and Purpose," with its bass and hypnotic, unsettling electro sample, is featured on LUNATIC SOUL. A beautiful ascent with Ray taking the lead, where things become much more interesting. A kind of GILDENLOW and pugnacious OSI hybrid, thanks to that captivating voice that makes all the difference. The ambient, intimate atmosphere makes you close your eyes and dream along to the edgy riff. "Enjoy The View" delves deeper into the electro-synthetic sound with its two-tone vocals and addictive instrumentation. The industrial riff, a sound effect on the thunderous breakdown, the keyboard undulating in a new dark-wave style. The magic works and endures with the energy of the invigorating chorus over the haunting verse, the haunting, dark outro. "Good Enough" features a crystalline, airy, stereo acoustic arpeggio reminiscent of the good old days. The raw, spoken-word vocals are laid over it, creating a country evening feel. The warm crescendo, with Ray as the sonic hero, evokes a dark Louisiana vibe with animals singing in the background: sublime and utterly simple, surfing on the atmospheric. "I'll Leave A Light On" kicks off with a fat riff, a melancholic nod to Katatonia. The pre-screamed vocals over the powerful sound, the chorus like something out of the mainstream era: the nostalgia is amplified by a punchy guitar solo bursting with notes. An added choir graces this track, which flows effortlessly, nothing new but well executed, finally on Fates Warning. "All Fall Away" boasts a bouncy bass beat. A dark, monolithic feel, redolent of Eurythmics in a heavy version, for this primal alternative drift. The guitar twists and turns, illuminating the space, the beat becomes oppressive, reminiscent of PARADISE LOST with Ray's voice, the chorus, then the beat abruptly stopping."Revenge," with its Wavy-esque guitar, surfs on the scales of THE CURE. This decadent rock descends to the realm of electro-pop, a softer DEPECHE MODE, Ray bribing his vocal cords. A repetitive, melancholic finale, far removed from prog rock. "Villains Or Saints" returns to mainstream, mainstream rock with its heavy melody, surfing once again on FATES WARNING. The haunting, synthetic rhythm builds and creates a heavy guitar space over the velvety keyboard. Ray conducts this masterful string piece, always effortless yet captivating, this timeless ballad. "What Is And What Was What," with its dark, ambient, mysterious intro and that wind that seems to come from nowhere. Vocals over a guitar arpeggio, choir over organ, hairs shiver. The bass resonates, clears the speakers, the pleasure of having this vibrant, body-piercing sound, like an arrow piercing your heart. "All That Comes After" returns to edgy rock, energized by its catchy melody. A B-side track that doesn't offer anything new, however, except perhaps to test the stereo image on the atmospheric drift. This melodic sound takes you back to the previous millennium. "How To Cast A Shadow" concludes, the new-wave vibe with its heady keyboard, as fat as the 'metroganic' drums, Ray weaving through this dark, hybrid, alternative slow jam. The mantra-like latency for dancing, swaying with his wife, the guitar both melancholic and slide-like. The feeling of navigating a bayou. A heavy guitar solo, the sound that makes you headbang, the refrain of 80s hard rock bands, I'm sucked into this musical spiral. The finale features Ray clinging to the primal synth, shh... Silence remains a constant presence throughout the album, with its enveloping notes.NORTH SEA ECHOES pushes their identity further with a heavy, dark approach, evolving with the addition of electronic elements to delve into the ghosts of the past, temptation, and reflection. (3.75)

items.body: The chorus of “Don’t Try” turns an old piece of street wisdom into a hook: “Don’t try piss on me and tell me it’s raining”. The man it is aimed at takes the credit for work he did not do, hands out promises that come to nothing, expects the overtime as standard and treats one late morning as an offence. Past him stand all the others: the smile that turns into a betrayal, the boasting about how easily things arrive, the liberties taken without a second thought. The last verse hands the accusation back, on the old line about the three fingers that point home whenever one goes out. Messenjah open Social Commentary with it, seven tracks of reggae made with The Aarons Brothers and released on Reload Records in April 2025. They have played roots reggae since forming in Kitchener, Ontario in 1981, and became the first Canadian reggae band signed to a major label when Warner Music Canada took Rock You High and put the music on national radio here for the first time. That was the second door Rupert “Ojiji” Harvey had opened, after Crack of Dawn, the Toronto soul group he co-founded, became the first Black Canadian band to sign a major deal. He has led Messenjah since the mid-1980s, through Reggae Sunsplash in Montego Bay, a Juno for Catch De Vibe, and a night in 1998 playing for Nelson Mandela at Toronto’s SkyDome. Hear “Don’t Try” HERE and pick up Social Commentary through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Messenjah & The Aarons Brothers – Don’t Try appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Zadisphere, an independent dark ritual techno project, published the video “Cathedral” on its official YouTube channel on September 9, 2026. Zadisphere makes a sound that mixes dark ritual techno with cinematic electronics and hypnotic rhythms, combining gothic and baroque elements, pipe organs, strings and choirs with analog sequences. “Cathedral” is a standalone video release; no tied single, EP or label has been confirmed. Zadisphere’s ‘Cathedral’ follows a steady run of new tracks “Cathedral” arrived in a run of near-weekly uploads from the project through August and September 2026, including “Czas / Time” on August 12, “Monolith Threshold” on September 1, “Ritual” on September 3, a remix of Ludwik Sempoliński’s “Ten wąsik” on September 11, “Nienazwane / Unnamed” on September 14 and “Po drugiej stronie / The other side” on September 16. No tracklist, formats or streaming availability have been confirmed for “Cathedral” beyond the YouTube upload. About Zadisphere Behind Zadisphere is a solo artist who treats mood and atmosphere as the project’s real subject, with sound built to serve that focus rather than the other way around. Its stated direction combines dark ritual techno, cinematic electronics and hypnotic rhythms with gothic and baroque influences, using pipe organs, strings, choirs and analog sequences. The project’s YouTube channel was created in January 2024, but its run of released tracks and videos began in August 2026 with “Czas / Time”, followed within weeks by “Monolith Threshold”, “Ritual” and “Cathedral”. Zadisphere has no confirmed label, Discogs entry or Wikipedia page. The project is also present on Instagram and maintains an official website. “Cathedral” is its latest video release.

items.body: chauncey, a Minneapolis-based synth-led alt-pop artist, released the single “Terrible Idea” on September 11, 2026. The chauncey “Terrible Idea” single is the first release from the seven-track album “Life of the Party,” due September 25, 2026. chauncey brings a synth-led alt-pop sound that mixes bright, impulsive hooks with a quieter, more reflective register, moving between crowded-room energy and the silence that follows once everyone has gone home. chauncey’s ‘Life of the Party’ album and ‘Terrible Idea’ “Life of the Party” traces a single night out, opening on anticipation and the people encountered along the way before turning to impulsive decisions and their comedown. chauncey has described the record as building toward “the empty room at the end,” once the crowd has gone. “Terrible Idea” takes on the impulsive side of that story, while “Permission” and “When Everybody Leaves” follow the aftermath, with the latter closing the record as the lights come back on. About chauncey chauncey is a Minneapolis-based artist who makes synth-led alt-pop, writing about crowded rooms, bad decisions and the quiet that sets in once everyone has gone. chauncey has kept the project’s origin story thin by choice, preferring the songs over a biography to do the introducing, and has summed up the approach as being a “kid with a synth.” The seven-track debut album “Life of the Party,” due September 25, 2026, follows a single night out from its opening rush to its final empty room. “Terrible Idea,” released September 11, 2026, is the album’s first single; “Permission” and “When Everybody Leaves” are among its other focus tracks. chauncey is based in Minneapolis.

items.body: Old Europa Cafe releases four new albums and three reissues on 23 October 2026, all as limited digipak CDs. The Italian power electronics, noise and dark ambient label, founded in Pordenone in 1983 by Rodolfo Protti, groups the batch around three reissues from the catalogue of Atrax Morgue, two new records tied to Swedish musician Nordvargr, and new albums from Black Leather Jesus and The Rita’s back catalogue. Atrax Morgue’s ‘Alive and Dead’, ‘Paranoia’ and ‘Pathophysiology’ reissued Atrax Morgue was the project of Marco Corbelli, an Italian noise musician born in Sassuolo in 1970 who died in 2007. Working mostly with a Sequential Circuits Six-Trak synthesizer, Corbelli built his early catalogue on cassette through the industrial and noise “cassette culture” of the early 1990s, releasing on his own Slaughter Productions before moving to labels including Old Europa Cafe, Relapse and RRRecords through the late 1990s. Old Europa Cafe reissues three Atrax Morgue titles on 23 October. ‘Alive and Dead’ is a CD re-edition of a cassette the label sold out in 2018, remastered by Devi(L)s Granziera (Teatro Satanico) and adding two previously unreleased live recordings, from Treviso in 1999 and Tokyo in 2006. ‘Paranoia’, originally Atrax Morgue’s first full-length CD album, released on Old Europa Cafe in 2000, returns in an expanded edition remastered by Devis G., adding two alternate versions of the track “Il Forcipe di Thanatos” first issued on the 2017 “Malaplacenta” 7-inch; those alternate versions stem from a 2007 recording session, the year of Corbelli’s death. ‘Pathophysiology’, first released as a 1995 cassette and reprinted on CDr in 2002 and CD in 2019, is remastered again at Sweet Slaughter for this edition, with four previously unreleased bonus tracks, two recorded in 1995 and two in 2002. Nordvargr powers new Apex Parasite and Fistfun records Swedish musician Henrik Nordvargr Björkk, known as Nordvargr, recorded and contributed vocals to Swedish power electronics act Apex Parasite‘s new album ‘Warzone Europa’, tracked at Nar Mattaru over July and August 2026. The album is released as a hand-numbered edition of 199 copies. Björkk, also known for his work with Mz.412, Folkstorm and Bøltorn, also appears on ‘Not Nice Ever’, a harsh noise collaboration released as Fistfun with Claudio Frassine, known for his projects Mademoiselle Bistouri and North Central. ‘Not Nice Ever’ follows the pair’s earlier Fistfun release “Up the Rolls” and is limited to 199 hand-numbered copies. Black Leather Jesus and The Rita round out the batch American industrial power noise project Black Leather Jesus, founded by Richard Ramirez in 1989, releases ‘Probe’ in a limited edition of 300 copies. The album’s core lineup features Sean E. Ramirez, Nathan Golub, Thomas Puopolo, Richard Ramirez, Kevin Novak, JRL, Anjilla Ulfhednar, Scott Kindberg and Domokos, with individual tracks built around guest collaborations with slowdanger, G.X. Jupitter-Larsen, Yellow Gas Flames and The Rita. The Rita, the harsh noise project of Canadian musician Sam McKinlay, credited on Discogs with originating the “harsh noise wall” style and coining the term, also gets a reissue in the batch. ‘Possessed Nun Sleaze’ was first released in 1998 on Labyrinth Recordings, in an edition of 50 cassette copies, marking The Rita’s first release on an American label. Old Europa Cafe’s CD reprint carries new artwork and is dedicated to Isabella and Sister Angela.

SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-lan
items.body: Valencia label Industrial Complexx reissues the various-artists compilation “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends” on double cassette and digital on October 15, 2026. The 18-track set, originally released by Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, gathers international minimal synth, electro-punk and industrial acts covering the catalogue of Suicide’s Alan Vega and Martin Rev. SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-language publication of “Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos,” an essay on the band by musician and writer Pedro Peñas y Robles, originally published in French and English in 2024 and now released in Spanish by Industrial Complexx. The book traces the duo’s genesis and the chaotic sessions behind their 1977 debut album, drawing on testimony from scene figures including Marc Hurtado of Étant Donnés. ‘SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends’ contributors The tribute pairs Vega and Rev’s original catalogue with reinterpretations from Distel, Radical G, The Horrorist, David Carretta and Jürgen Engler of Die Krupps, Növö, Adan+Ilse featuring Gabi Delgado of D.A.F., Marc Hurtado performing with Alan Vega himself, Liebknecht featuring Kristoffer Grip of Agent Side Grinder, Unknown Celebrities, Laag, Position Parallele, Cruise [ctrl] featuring Richard 23 and Patrick Codenys of Front 242, The Present Moment, Absolute Body Control, Millimetric featuring Dirk Da Davo of The Neon Judgement, Black Egg featuring hausfrau, Simi Nah featuring KGB, and In Death It Ends featuring Usher of Norma Loy. Covered songs include “Che,” “Ghost Rider,” “Cheree,” “Frankie Teardrop,” “Dream Baby Dream” and “Diamonds, Fur Coat, Champagne.” Industrial Complexx describes the collection as channeling “the same abrasive, alienating and futuristic energy” that shaped Suicide’s catalogue. About Suicide Suicide was an American duo formed in New York City in 1970 by vocalist Alan Vega and instrumentalist Martin Rev, initially a trio with guitarist Paul Liebgott before continuing as a two-piece. The group paired Vega’s stream-of-conscious, rockabilly-inflected vocals with Rev’s minimal synthesizer and drum-machine backing, and was among the first acts to use the term “punk music” to describe itself, in 1970. Suicide independently released its debut album, “Suicide,” in 1977 on Red Star Records, featuring “Ghost Rider,” “Frankie Teardrop” and “Cheree.” A second album, “Suicide: Alan Vega and Martin Rev,” followed in 1980 on Ze Records, then “A Way of Life” in 1988, “Why Be Blue” in 1992 and the final studio album, “American Supreme,” in 2002. Vega and Rev also worked separately: Vega collaborated with Andrew Eldritch of The Sisters of Mercy as The Sisterhood in 1986, and with Alex Chilton and Ben Vaughn on “Cubist Blues” in 1996, while both released solo albums throughout their careers. Suicide played its final concert at London’s Barbican Centre on July 9, 2015, before Alan Vega died on July 16, 2016, at age 78. “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends,” first released via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, returns via Industrial Complexx on October 15, 2026, alongside the Spanish edition of Pedro Peñas y Robles’s book on the band.

items.body: Black Tape For A Blue Girl and Projekt Records reissue “The Rope” on October 2, presenting the 1986 debut album in a limited edition that pairs the original mix, remastered, with a new 2026 mix by Sam Rosenthal for its 40th anniversary. The 2LP edition is limited to 300 copies on 140-gram vinyl, with LP1 pressed on baby blue vinyl with black splatters and LP2 on transparent blue vinyl with white splatters. A 2CD digipak edition adds seven bonus tracks. Both formats are released via Projekt Records. “The Rope” is Black Tape For A Blue Girl’s debut album, the project Sam Rosenthal built around his songwriting and electronics, with Oscar Herrera on vocals. Each format includes the full 12-track album twice: the original 1986 mix, remastered, and the new 2026 mix. Martin Bowes of Attrition handled the mastering. The 2LP package adds a 16-page lyric and memorabilia fanzine insert plus a sticker; the 2CD edition comes in a 6-panel digipak with a 4-panel photo insert and sticker. The original 1986 tracklist runs: “memory, uncaring friend”, “hide in yourself”, “within these walls”, “the holy terrors”, “end”, “seven days til sunrise”, “the rope”, “the few remaining threads”, “the lingering flicker”, “slow blur”, “the floor was hard but home” and “we return”. The 2CD edition adds seven bonus tracks exclusive to that format: “the lingering flicker (first draft)”, “within these walls (early mix with clarinet)”, “the holy terrors (long)”, “second dream”, “the lingering flicker (isolated violins)”, “within these walls (short with violins)” and “memory, uncaring friend (remix intro)”. Sam Rosenthal on writing ‘The Rope’ Black Tape For A Blue Girl’s Rosenthal, who also founded Projekt Records, described the circumstances that produced the album: “In November ’85, following two years of recording instrumental electronic music, I invited Oscar Herrera to sing two songs on my ISLANDS cassette. A few months later in February of ’86 I left Florida for college in Orange, California. I was 20 years old, feeling isolated, lonely, missing friends back home. In my dorm room that spring I used the school’s Fostex 250 4-track cassette portastudio to record songs with my lyrics and melodies. Writing words for Oscar to sing over my ethereal and ambient music helped me explore those angsty and tangled feelings. The Rope is half vocal and half instrumental. It’s all quite minimal, yet it’s an album listeners still mention as a favorite. Capturing the confusion and darkness I felt at that time remains valid; new listeners connect with it today. I never would have expected that 40 years later The Rope would be listened to and appreciated by new generations. It’s really nice knowing those feelings are timeless, and the music has a place in people’s lives.” Uncut included “The Rope” in its “200 Greatest Goth Albums” feature, describing it as: “The vehicle for the more electronic songwriting of Projekt Records’ founder Sam Rosenthal, brought to life by singer Oscar Herrera’s arch delivery. BTFABG spun a unique thread of ambient darkwave, neoclassical exoticism and dark cabaret on their relatively bare-boned and lo-fi debut album.” The Rope (40th) by Black Tape For A Blue Girl About Black Tape For A Blue Girl Black Tape For A Blue Girl is the project Sam Rosenthal formed in 1986, built around his own songwriting and electronics and centered from the start on the pairing of his instrumental, ambient compositions with vocalists singing his lyrics. “The Rope”, released that year on Projekt Records, the label Rosenthal founded, introduced Oscar Herrera as vocalist alongside contributions from Allan Kraut, Kim Prior, Adam Buhler, Candy Sherlock and Lara Radford. The project’s discography continued through “Mesmerized by the Sirens” (1987), “Ashes in the Brittle Air” (1989), “A Chaos of Desire” (1991), “This Lush Garden Within” (1993), “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” (1996), “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” (1999), “The Scavenger Bride” (2002), “Halo Star” (2004), “10 Neurotics” (2009), “Tenderotics” (2013), “These Fleeting Moments” (2016), “To Touch the Milky Way” (2018) and “The Cleft Serpent” (2021). Projekt has revisited several of these titles as anniversary reissues in recent years, including “The Cleft Serpent” and “Ashes in the Brittle Air” on vinyl, “Mesmerized by the Sirens” on vinyl and double CD, and “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” and “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” in their own anniversary editions. Rosenthal has also continued to release music outside the project, including ambient and drone recordings under his own name. The 40th anniversary edition of “The Rope” extends that reissue campaign to the album that started it, presenting Herrera’s original vocal performances and Rosenthal’s 1986 arrangements alongside his 2026 revisiting of the same material.
