items.excerpt: Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart reissue the 2xCD collection “The Usual Suspects” on Dimple Discs on November 13, 2026. Originally released in 2017, the 23-track set has been unavailable for years and now changes hands at collectors’ prices; the digital edition is already available on Bandcamp, with the physical 2xCD prepared for that November date to coincide with a UK and Belgium tour. Usual Suspects by Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart “The Usual Suspec
items.body: Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart reissue the 2xCD collection “The Usual Suspects” on Dimple Discs on November 13, 2026. Originally released in 2017, the 23-track set has been unavailable for years and now changes hands at collectors’ prices; the digital edition is already available on Bandcamp, with the physical 2xCD prepared for that November date to coincide with a UK and Belgium tour. Usual Suspects by Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart “The Usual Suspects” gathers new recordings of Wobble’s solo material alongside songs from Invaders Of The Heart and his former band Public Image Ltd (PiL), drawn from a catalogue spanning almost forty years at the time of recording. The album was recorded at The Smokehouse studios in East London and opens with a version of PiL’s debut single “Public Image”, reworked from the band’s 1978 debut album. The tracklist also folds in cover versions of two film themes, “Midnight Cowboy” and “Get Carter”, plus Dawn Penn’s “You Don’t Love Me (No, No, No)” featuring vocalist Aurora Dawn, and a new take on “Visions Of You”, which originally featured Sinéad O’Connor on Invaders Of The Heart’s Mercury Prize-nominated 1992 album “Rising Above Bedlam”. The set closes with live recordings of “Liquidator” and “Poptones”, the latter drawn from PiL’s “Metal Box”. Recording personnel on “The Usual Suspects” comprised Jah Wobble on bass, vocals and percussion, Marc Layton-Bennett on drums, percussion and backing vocals, Martin Chung on guitars, George King on keyboards and backing vocals, Steve Rigby on programming and backing vocals, Sean Corby on trumpet and flugelhorn, Aurora Dawn on vocals, and Holly Macve on vocals. Of the band behind the album, Wobble said: “This band has been a delight to play with. Similar to my first early ’80s version of the Invaders, they can all really play, plus all genre bases […] are covered. It’s a big deal to me, because it’s like a 35 year old dream has finally been realised. This is how I heard The Invaders of the Heart sound all those years ago. A classy fusion of genres. Groovy, dubby but always changing and developing. Never standing still.” Tour dates for Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart The reissue follows a UK tour and comes ahead of Belgian dates in November. Confirmed shows: October 3 – Stourbridge, Katie Fitzgerald’s (UK) October 16 – Todmorden, Unitarian Church (UK) October 21 – Frome, The Tunnels (UK) October 22 – Bristol, The Fleece (UK) October 23 – Reading, Face Bar (UK) November 7 – London, Bush Hall (UK) November 25 – Hasselt, Club AFF (Belgium) November 26 – Bruges, Cactus Muziekcentrum (Belgium) November 27 – Oudenaarde, Harmonie Oudenaarde (Belgium) Tickets are available via Songkick. About Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart Jah Wobble, born John Wardle, is a bass guitarist and vocalist from East London who was the original bassist in Public Image Ltd alongside John Lydon from the band’s 1978 formation, co-writing and playing on the 1979 album “Metal Box” before leaving in late 1980. He formed Jah Wobble’s Invaders Of The Heart in 1982; that same period brought studio work alongside Can’s Holger Czukay and Jaki Liebezeit, U2 guitarist The Edge, and producer François Kevorkian. Invaders Of The Heart’s commercial peak came with 1991’s “Rising Above Bedlam”, nominated for the Mercury Prize, which included the UK top-40 single “Visions Of You” featuring Sinéad O’Connor. Wobble has since worked with artists including Ginger Baker, Björk, Brian Eno, Baaba Maal, Massive Attack, Sinéad O’Connor, Pharoah Sanders and his wife Zi Lan Liao on guzheng and harp. He reunited with former PiL guitarist Keith Levene in 2012 for the “Metal Box in Dub” shows and the album “Yin & Yang”. Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart recorded “The Usual Suspects” at The Smokehouse studios in East London, releasing it in 2017 following a six-month UK tour, as covered by Side-Line at the time. More recently, Wobble released the albums “Dub, Vol 1” (2025) and “Automated Paradise” (2026, with former Siouxsie & The Banshees guitarist Jon Klein) on Dimple Discs, and “Mystic Liverpool: The Beatles Psychedelic Songbook” with his sons, who record as Tian Qiyi, released by Cherry Red in August 2026. His autobiography, “Memoirs of a Geezer: Music, Life, Mayhem”, was published by Serpent’s Tail in 2009 and reissued in expanded form as “Dark Luminosity” by Faber & Faber in 2024. Dimple Discs now reissues “The Usual Suspects” as a 2xCD on November 13, 2026, timed to Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart’s UK and Belgium tour dates.

The two-track release pairs the title track with “Do not leave a message” and arrives while the duo works on a new album. items.body: Room of Wires, the UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers who both go by Andrew, released the single “Skin weevil” on September 18, 2026, self-released on Bandcamp. The two-track release pairs the title track with “Do not leave a message” and arrives while the duo works on a new album. Skin weevil by Room of Wires Room of Wires bring an industrial and electronic sound that mixes hard-hitting rhythm programming with the duo’s usual dark ambient textures and field recordings. Both tracks on “Skin weevil” were written and produced by Room of Wires; the cover artwork is by the duo as well, with performance for camera by Fenia Kotsopoulou and photography by Daz Disley. Room of Wires’ ‘Skin weevil’ single The duo has not met in person: one member works with hardware and a tangle of physical wires, the other in software and virtual cables, sharing ideas and sounds over the internet. That process has produced “Skin weevil” as a standalone two-track single rather than part of a longer EP or album, released independently while the pair continue work on their next full-length. No further tracks or release date for that album have been announced. About Room of Wires Room of Wires is a UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers, both named Andrew, who write and record without ever having met, exchanging sounds and ideas remotely. Their debut EP, “Asylum sneaker”, appeared on Section27 in August 2014, followed by the Bandcamp-only “Dead skins” EP in November 2015, “Used as a runner” on Section27 in June 2016, “Black medicine” on Section27 in June 2017, and the remix-featuring “Mastakink” EP, self-released in October 2017. Their debut album, “White transit”, followed in November 2018, and the mini-LP “Test subject” arrived in October 2019. Room of Wires signed to the German label ant-zen for the albums “Plague of people” (April 2021) and “Welcome to the end game” (February 2023), releasing the “Fever switch” EP on Rednetic in October 2021 in between. Further self-released EPs followed with “Floodplains” (November 2023) and the album “If no other means are effective” in December 2025, the duo’s first full-length in close to three years. Alongside their own catalogue, Room of Wires record collaborative material as DasF and Cave like carving, and have contributed remixes and tracks to releases by Ah Cama-Sotz, Flint Glass, 4T Thieves and other acts. “Skin weevil” is their first new material since 2025’s “If no other means are effective”, released as the pair continue work on a new Room of Wires album.

items.body: Nine Inch Nails released their third studio album, “The Fragile,” through Nothing Records and Interscope Records on 21 September 1999. The industrial rock record arrived as a double album of 23 tracks running one hour and 43 minutes, split across two discs titled “Left” and “Right.” It turns 27 this year. Five years separated “The Fragile” from “The Downward Spiral.” Trent Reznor recorded and mixed the album at Nothing Studios in New Orleans between 1997 and 1999, producing it with Alan Moulder, who also engineered and mixed. Steve Albini handled supplemental drum recording at his Electrical Audio in Chicago, Tom Baker mastered at Precision Mastering, and Bob Ezrin was credited for final continuity and flow. Dr. Dre assisted with the mix on “Even Deeper.” Danny Lohner played guitars on six tracks and contributed drum programming and synthesizers, Adrian Belew added guitar to “Just Like You Imagined,” “The Great Below” and “Where Is Everybody?”, and Mike Garson played piano on “Just Like You Imagined,” “The Way Out Is Through” and “Ripe (With Decay).” Bill Rieflin drummed on “La Mer” alongside vocalist Denise Milfort, Jerome Dillon supplied chorus drums on “We’re in This Together,” and Charlie Clouser, Keith Hillebrandt and Steve Duda covered programming and sound design. David Carson took art direction, design and photography. Disc one, “Left,” runs “Somewhat Damaged,” “The Day the World Went Away,” “The Frail,” “The Wretched,” “We’re in This Together,” “The Fragile,” “Just Like You Imagined,” “Even Deeper,” “Pilgrimage,” “No, You Don’t,” “La Mer” and “The Great Below.” Disc two, “Right,” runs “The Way Out Is Through,” “Into the Void,” “Where Is Everybody?”, “The Mark Has Been Made,” “Please,” “Starfuckers, Inc.,” “Complication,” “I’m Looking Forward to Joining You, Finally,” “The Big Come Down,” “Underneath It All” and “Ripe (With Decay).” Three singles came from the album: “The Day the World Went Away” on 20 July 1999, “We’re in This Together” on 27 September 1999 and “Into the Void” on 10 January 2000, with “Starfuckers, Inc.” issued as a promotional single. The album entered the Billboard 200 at number one with first-week sales of 229,000 copies, the band’s first chart-topping album, then fell to number 16 the following week. The RIAA certified it double platinum on 4 January 2000, and it had sold 898,000 copies in the United States by May 2005. The US edition appeared as a two-CD tri-fold digipak; the three-LP vinyl pressing carried two tracks absent from the CD, “10 Miles High” and “The New Flesh,” and came in a gatefold sleeve with a 24-page booklet. In 2017 the album was reissued on vinyl as a Definitive Edition alongside “The Fragile: Deviations 1,” a limited four-LP instrumental set that was not pressed to CD. The album streams on Spotify. Sources differ on the exact day: MusicBrainz lists 20 September 1999, while Wikipedia, Discogs and Spotify all give 21 September 1999. About Nine Inch Nails Trent Reznor formed Nine Inch Nails in Cleveland, Ohio in 1988, writing and recording the project’s material during off-hours at Right Track Studio, where he worked as an engineer and janitor. TVT Records issued the debut album, “Pretty Hate Machine,” on 20 October 1989. The “Broken” EP followed in 1992, by which point Reznor had negotiated the Nothing Records imprint through Interscope, and “The Downward Spiral” arrived in 1994. Side-Line covered the 2019 book “Into The Never”, which examined that album’s cultural reach, and reported that Johnny Cash initially resisted recording “Hurt”, the “Downward Spiral” track he covered in 2002. “The Fragile” closed the 1990s for the band, and the remix album “Things Falling Apart” followed in 2000. Reznor returned with “With Teeth” in 2005, “Year Zero” in 2007, and both “Ghosts I-IV” and “The Slip” in 2008. Atticus Ross became a full member ahead of “Hesitation Marks” in 2013, and the pair have scored film and television alongside the band since. Side-Line has since reported on Reznor’s appearance on the deluxe vinyl reissue of the 1990 Pigface debut, the Future Ruins festival announced by Reznor and Ross in 2025, the “TRON Ares: Divergence” companion album, and the “Nine Inch Noize” collaboration with Boys Noize released in April 2026. “The Fragile” turns 27 this year, the record that took the band to number one in the United States for the first time.

items.body: Clan of Xymox, the Dutch darkwave and gothic rock project led by Ronny Moorings, released “Notes From The Underground” on 21 September 2001 through Pandaimonium Records in Europe. The album turns 25 this year. Metropolis Records issued it in North America nine days later, on 30 September 2001. Moorings wrote, recorded and mixed all twelve tracks, and produced the record with Mojca Zugna. It was the third studio album of the reformed Clan of Xymox era, after “Hidden Faces” from 1997 and “Creatures” from 1999. Three of its songs were already in circulation by the time it appeared. The “Liberty” CD single, issued by Pandaimonium on 20 October 2000 alongside the band’s double live album, carried “Liberty” together with “Number One” and “At Your Mercy”. Clan of Xymox’s ‘Notes From The Underground’ tracklist and credits The CD runs twelve tracks: “Innocent”, “I Want You Now”, “Internal Darkness”, “At Your Mercy”, “Anguish”, “Number One”, “Into Her Web”, “The Bitter Sweet”, “Liberty”, “Something Wrong”, “Mysterium” and “The Same Dream”. Dierk Budde mastered the album and Mojca Zugna made the sleeve artwork. The band’s official biography states the record reached number 2 on the German DAC chart and topped the US Musicfolio poll for 2001. The same page quotes a Side-Line review of the album as reading “This album is to be seen as a milestone in the band’s discography towards which their previous efforts all converge, or emerge from.” Pandaimonium returned to the material in May 2002 with “Remixes From The Underground”, a two-disc set that reworked every song on the album. Its contributors included Front 242, Assemblage 23, In Strict Confidence, Iris, Angels & Agony and Beborn Beton, and the limited edition added the band’s first video disc. Notes from the Underground by Clan Of Xymox About Clan of Xymox Ronny Moorings formed the band in 1981 in Nijmegen, the Netherlands. Its first release, the mini-album “Subsequent Pleasures”, appeared in 1983 in a run of 500 copies recorded on a four-track home setup. Demo material sent with it led to a deal with 4AD, and the self-titled album followed in 1985, cut at Palladium Studios in Edinburgh and co-produced with label head Ivo Watts-Russell. “Medusa” came next on the same label, and the band contributed “Muscoviet Musquito” to the 4AD compilation “Lonely Is An Eyesore” in 1987. The group parted with 4AD in October 1988, signed to Wing, a PolyGram subsidiary, and shortened its name to Xymox. “Twist of Shadows” arrived in 1989 with the singles “Obsession”, “Imagination” and “Blind Hearts”; the band’s official biography puts its sales above 300,000 copies. “Phoenix” followed in 1991 and closed the Wing chapter when PolyGram wound the label down. “Metamorphosis” and “Headclouds” then came out on the UK independent Zok Records. Moorings also wrote music for two CD-ROM games in the same period, “Total Mayhem” in 1996 and “Revenant” a year later. In 1997 Moorings ended the Xymox era, restarted the band as Clan of Xymox and signed to Tess Records. “Hidden Faces” appeared that year, produced by Dave M. Allen and John A. Rivers. “Creatures” followed in 1999, mixed by Rivers and Moorings, and moved the band to Metropolis Records in North America and Pandaimonium Records in Europe, the pairing that would also handle “Notes From The Underground”. The double live album “LIVE”, drawn from the band’s South and Central American shows, came out in October 2000. “Farewell” arrived in 2003, and “The Best Of Clan Of Xymox”, with its running order chosen by a fan poll, in September 2004. The “Weak In My Knees” EP opened 2006 ahead of the album “Breaking Point”. In early 2009 the band moved to Trisol Records in Europe while staying with Metropolis in the United States, and “In Love We Trust” came out on 18 August 2009, covered in Clan of Xymox’s ‘In Love We Trust’ turns 17 on 18 August. The thirteenth studio album “Darkest Hour” followed on 20 May 2011, the covers set “Kindred Spirits” in October 2012 and “Matters Of Mind, Body And Soul” on 14 February 2014. “Days Of Black” arrived on 7 April 2017, reported in Clan Of Xymox return with new album: ‘Days Of Black’. “Spider On The Wall” followed in 2020, announced in New Clan Of Xymox album ‘Spider On The Wall’ and video for ‘All I Ever Know’, and Moorings talked through his writing that September in Interview with Clan Of Xymox: ‘For Me A Lot Of These Memories Are Finished Stories Without A Soundtrack’. “Limbo”, written during the pandemic lockdowns, arrived in July 2021 and was previewed in Clan Of Xymox returns with all new album ‘Limbo’ in July. The eighteenth album “Exodus” followed in June 2024, reported in Clan Of Xymox announce new album for June: ‘Exodus’, with the “Blood of Christ” EP later that year and a 3CD edition of “Exodus” in February 2025. Moorings looked back across the full run in Ronny Moorings (Clan Of Xymox), an exclusive retrospective interview. Moorings has been the only constant member and still writes, records and produces the band’s music. The live line-up is Moorings on vocals, guitar and melodica, Mojca Zugna on bass, Mario Usai on guitar and bass, and Sean Winzer on keyboards, synth drums and backing vocals. Twenty-five years on, “Notes From The Underground” sits between “Creatures” and “Farewell” in that sequence.

items.body: Bristol project Allflaws released the album The Age Of Nefarious on September 21, 2026, through UK independent label Derelict State Records. The album runs 14 tracks over one hour and one minute, and is available to buy on iTunes and Amazon. Allflaws is the work of Gabriel Curran, who mixes industrial hip hop, trip hop, breakbeat, electronica and dark electronic music on “The Age Of Nefarious”. The album keeps heavy beats, distorted textures and atmospheric production under raw rap vocals, its atmosphere stays tied to Bristol trip hop, but the record leans harder into industrial hip hop’s heavier low end and lets experimental electronica break the production into fractured, glitching textures. Derelict State Records describes the album’s lyrics as exploring control, conformity, digital identity, cultures of violence, low-trust societies, and human resilience. Allflaws’ ‘The Age Of Nefarious’ pushes past the Bristol trip hop sound Derelict State Records, the independent UK label operating out of Bristol and London, works across trip hop, electronica, dub, breakbeat and the darker end of industrial music, including industrial hip hop, industrial electro and EBM. “The Age Of Nefarious” is distributed by Catapult, the same distributor behind Allflaws’ catalog since its earliest releases. An album trailer for “The Age Of Nefarious” is also online on YouTube. Side-Line previously covered Allflaws’ recent standalone singles, including “Vanity Matrix” in 2025, “Chimera” in 2024, and “Antifragile” in 2023. About Allflaws Allflaws was established in Bristol in 2004 by Gabriel Curran, who remains its only official member, writing, producing and performing every release. Curran’s vocal style combines rapping and singing with dark, poetic lyrics, and the project has built its sound around industrial, trip hop and breakbeat elements since its start. Allflaws signed to Catapult and Derelict State Records and released the album “These Walls Are Lies” in 2007, followed by the EPs “Ghost Of The System” and “Replicant Breed” and the album “Black Box Here After” in 2009. The singles “Escaping Sanity” (2010), “Amrak” (2011) and “Interfearence” (2011) preceded the “R Complex” EP and the single “Manufactured Violence” in 2012, and the album “Versus The Soul” in 2013. The album “Apparitions” followed in 2016, then “Mysterium” in 2019 and “Arcana” in 2021. Allflaws released the EP “Ghostrumentals” and the single “Becoming” in 2022, and the single “Antifragile” in 2024. “The Age Of Nefarious”, released September 21, 2026 on Derelict State Records, is Allflaws’ latest full-length, continuing the project’s industrial hip hop and trip hop direction two decades into Curran’s run with Allflaws.

items.body: This is Decca’s eighth release featuring Lise Davidsen, following hard on the heels of a Live at the Met recording released earlier this year. This is her first album devoted to Verdi, and it includes scenes from Macbeth, Un ballo in maschera, La forza del destino, Don Carlo and Aida. Verdi Amazon Presto Apple As readers surely know, Davidsen is considered by many to be one of today’s greatest operatic sopranos. The Metropolitan Opera’s Peter Gelb describes her as “the greatest Wagnerian talent since Birgit Nilsson and Kirsten Flagstad,” and conductor Antonio Pappano describes her voice as “one-in-a-million.” The singing on this album makes it hard to argue with such superlatives: Davidsen has tremendous power and consistency across an extended vocal range, although her control is such that she produces an impressively soft, silvery color when needed. The many high climactic notes heard in this recital ring out with a glistening brilliance that few can match. Yet despite this superb technique, not everything proved moving. I should acknowledge that I am not a fan of these “bleeding chunks” recitals. The publicity argues that there is a coherent framework for the selections, an exploration of the “emotional worlds of five remarkable women.” But with several selections lasting less than five minutes, a stop-and-start engagement is inevitable. The London Philharmonic plays wonderfully, with lots of energy, but sometimes there seems to be a generalized emotional mood from the podium that lessens the partnership between orchestra and singer. An impressive version of Nel dì della vittoria (track 1) opens the program. Davidsen captures the dark manipulative drive of Lady Macbeth, yet in Shirley Verrett’s two performances (La Scala/Abbado/DG and Teatro Comunale di Bologna/Chailly/Decca) I find an even more vivid characterization, even if Verrett’s is less opulent than Davidsen’s, and both Abbado and Chailly find more menace in the score. Lise Davidsen. Photo © Fredrik Arff. The three selections from Un ballo in maschera are more captivating (the orchestra also plays the Prelude to Act II, track 6). Both Ma dall’arido (track 8) and Morrò, ma prima in grazia (track 9) demonstrate Davidsen’s superb vocal control. In the latter she finds a heart-breaking vulnerability as she begs to see and hold her son before she dies (Kristina Blaumane’s cello solo adds to the potency of this aria). The accompaniment seems more engaged throughout these scenes. The selections from Don Carlo are excellent, though I find Callas’s willingness to act, even at the expense of vocal beauty, even more compelling. And I would be hard pressed to argue that Davidsen is more affecting or beautiful than Montserrat Caballé’s recording with the Covent Garden forces led by Carlo Maria Giulini (Warner Classics). The emotional temperature rises with the involvement of the Apollo Voices chorus in two selections from La forza del destino: La vergine degli angeli (track 11) is the most moving performance on the album. The recital closes with a wonderful reading of Ritorna vincitor! (track 15) from Aida, yet it does not eclipse Leontyne Price’s reading from her recording with forces from the Rome Opera House conducted by Solti (Decca). Despite the caveats mentioned above, this is an impressive achievement and there is no doubt that Davidsen’s many admirers will snap this up. It should also prove attractive to listeners who have yet to hear this uniquely gifted singer. Decca’s booklet is still unavailable on most digital media, which keeps many listeners from accessing full texts and context for recital programs like this one. items.body: One half of the Senior Staff was able to get out to a wholly non-ID:UD related gig over the weekend and catch Calgary’s Mares Of Thrace play a very rhythmically tight and cathartic set of doom metal. As we’ve briefly discussed here and there we’re both fans of a decent amount of metal covering a number of sub-genres, but neither of us are experts. Frankly, sometimes its nice to switch off the part of your brain that needs to be developing informed opinions and producing thoughtful analysis at all times and just enjoy some music simply because you dig it. But speaking of thoughtful analysis (?), let’s get you back to the home front with this week’s tracks. Dismantled Godflesh, “Master And Slave” Justin Broadrick announced earlier this year that he’d be winding Godflesh down for a second time some fifteen-odd years after its reactivation, but was planning two full LPs of new material before that time comes. The first such record sees release on Friday, and while the ratio of dub, electronic, and breaks elements which have always flitted about Godflesh releases had perhaps increased over the last few post-reunion albums, it’s hard not to think that Decay will be going right for the jugular Streetcleaner style based on its opening track. Turn it up and revel in the soothing annihilation of that bass tone. Decay by GODFLESH Grendel, “Dominion” It’s somehow been 7 years since the release of Grendel’s last LP Ascending the Abyss. It’s been a tangible absence in Our offices; JD Tucker has spent the last decade and a half redefining his legacy as an electro-industrial stylist and producer, starting with 2012’s genre-defying Timewave: Zero and the superlative Age of the Disposable Body, the latter being legitimately one of the most important political albums of the 2010s in Our Thing. “Dominion” speaks to the band we’ve come to know Grendel to be while showing some intriguing developments, such as JD’s now accomplished melodic vocal style, some very smooth string programming and sleek modern sound design applied to a classic EBM gallop. All that and lyrics that don’t just decry the social media era but examine the panopticon of control they emerge from? Welcome back Grendel, we missed you. Dominion by Grendel Dismantled, “Zero” Speaking of long-awaited returns, holy shit, there’s new Dismantled. Gary Zon’s long-running project has always been a standard bearer for a version of hard and harsh electro-industrial that maintains the genre’s atmospheric and emotional core. The first track from the forthcoming Endless is “Zero”, a cut that features Zon’s distinctive processed and multi-layered vocals, samples, and some fine string programming for good measure. It’s melancholic, but after a more than half a decade wait (the album was originally teased all the way back in 2021), it’s a sound that feels right. Endless by Dismantled Rosetta Stone, “Shadowban” Porl King’s moved Rosetta Stone through a number of preceding modes since reactivating the legendary second wave of goth rock project as a solo joint seven years back. A forthcoming release looks to keep that trend going (the Executing Nostalgia title feels rather on the nose in that regard) – one half of it will be made up of classic goth covers, continuing in the tradition of Unerotica and last year’s Nothing Is Sacred, while the other half is originals. This first taste of the latter feels like a callback to a very different moment in King’s history, though: the claustrophobic and hazy bass fog of this cut’s a dead ringer for the post witch house loops and grooves which made up the bulk of the voluminous In Death It Ends catalog in the 2010s. Shadowban by Rosetta Stone Control Fields, “Black Anomaly” Some solidly chewy bass sits at the centre of the B-side of the debut single from Tbilisi producer Control Fields, but that’s not the only thing which has us flashing back to 90s EBM and dark electro. The combo of icy programming and classic “hacking the Gibson” style sampling on this goes down as smooth as a Jolt cola being slammed during an all night Quake LAN party. Friction Code by Control Fields Emmon, “Relics (Kris Baha remix)” Kris Baha is one of the most reliable producers that emerged from the techno-body moment, with his canny grasp of gnarly sound design and how to assemble peak time bangers making him a go-to remixer for many artists. For evidece of why and the results why not check out Baha’s mix for Emmon’s “Relics”, taking the pensive and punchy original and giving it a slick peak-time makeover that references breakbeat driven 90’s techno, some psytrance, and some seriously warped synthwork. This’ll singe your nosehairs if you aren’t careful, play loud with caution. The post Tracks: September 21st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Band: Kraanerg | Album: Aria for Labellum Tongues | Genre: Avant-prog | Year: 2026 From: Minneapolis, USA | Label: Independent For fans of: Frank Zappa, Papangu, Sigh, Cardiacs Bandcamp Kraanerg is the brainchild of composer and multi-instrumentalist Nat Bergrin, and Aria for Labellum Tongues is their third full-length release (and their second as a full band). This was my first exposure to Kraanerg, and I was very impressed by what I encountered. Western classical music plays a massive role on this record, both in terms of instrumentation and structure. Plenty of bands will shoehorn in some violin, but not many display the ability to integrate classical influences quite like this band does. “Amargosa Raga” kicks the album off with strange, discordant guitar lines. The vocal line is surprisingly melodic for the harsh, microtonal backing, and there’s some great supporting saxophone. Classical elements play a significant role here as well, with violin and piano taking the lead on various passages. What began as a fairly harsh piece gradually evolves into a lush composition, evoking many of the Mellotron-heavy greats of the classic prog era, but run through a more modern and uncompromisingly weird lens. The title track comes next, with an onslaught of buzzy guitars, swooping strings, and tinkling vibraphone. The classical influences on this track tread a fine line between sweet and creepy, with the violin frequently adding a remorseful edge.  “Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji” nearly feels like a new wave song in its opening moments. There’s a bright hopefulness, but that soon gives way to a stripped-back classical passage. Piano, violin, and scratchy clean guitar float about. The intensity of the song gradually swells with the addition of drums and wordless vocals, lifting everything upward, but with an underlying sense of tension. When rock elements eventually take the lead again, violin remains the most prominent instrument. There’s an irrepressible sense of drama, and the somewhat rough vocals feel genuinely emotional. This piece is followed by the only song under four minutes on the album, “Anguloa Virginalis (Um Rosto de Mulher)”. It’s a light and airy breather following the intensity of the previous song. Piano, vibraphone, and delicate percussion evoke loungey jazz. Gothic organ and distorted guitar kicks off “Iron Sign of the Masdevallia”. Syncopated drums and piano give this track a disorienting feel, and the dense arrangement is smothering. As the song enters an instrumental section, sax and piano both get ample time in the spotlight, each one painting a dramatic picture. Next, the song takes a surprisingly sunny turn, with piano plinking out over a (mostly) major-key backing. The guitars borrow a lot from punk, but just about everything else is more clearly indebted to classical music, which makes for an interesting contrast. This artsy punk-fusion continues as this epic enters its final few minutes. The chords become more chaotic and irregular, and the vocals become more unhinged. The music is intense, yet oddly joyous, like Cardiacs’ best work. The opening gothic passage comes back for a closing reprise, which ties things up beautifully. The album ends on its longest song, the 20-minute “Visible to the Wrong Faces”. In comparison to the storming tempo of the previous song, this one is quite restrained in its opening. Classical music predominates for the first few minutes, led by piano and saxophone. It isn’t until about four minutes in that any rock elements enter, when buzzing guitars and stomping drums begin to play supporting roles. When vocals finally enter, the music is noisy with a sense of carefully-crafted chaos. Vibraphone and violin support jangly, post-punk guitars, and the vocal melody draws from avant-garde music. Throughout this whole album, the band has shown that they are masters of textural variation and contrast, and the second half of this song is a prime example. Post-metal, classical music, and classic prog influences are all evident, and everything gels into a satisfying conclusion. Aria for Labellum Tongues is a highly ambitious and very successful musical statement. The blending of rock and classical structures is pulled off wonderfully, and each of the songs on this album feels thoughtfully put-together. It’s a long and challenging record, but it’s well worth your time. Score: 95/100

items.excerpt: Am I capable of writing about music without referencing Eurovision? items.body: Am I capable of writing about music without referencing Eurovision? I guess not, especially if the band in question legitimately competed in a recent edition of my beloved song contest. By charming over 76,000 voters with an atmospheric blend of Nordic folk rock, Gåte won the 62nd Melodi Grand Prix, subsequently leading to their appearance at the Eurovision Song Contest 2024, representing Norway. Despite moving on from their allotted semifinal, the group placed dead last amongst the twenty-five finalists. The chaotic performance of their song "Ulveham" didn't impress international audiences or the professional jury, but it sure as hell made an impact on one American Eurofan, and the consensus among hardcore watchers is that Gåte was brutally robbed. After their undeserved flop, Gåte retreated to the forests of Norway for two years, finally reemerging with Sigil—a grander full-length to rekindle the sylvan aura they condensed and presented to over a hundred million people in just three minutes. I like to think of Gåte like a wreath. The center is vocalist Gunnhild Sundli. Her vocalizations—whether singing or chanting—have an unmistakable inflection that drifts over each piece with both tenderness and command. When she dips down into her lower register, the atmosphere turns foggy, but when Sundli lifts her tones high she effortlessly clears the fog to reveal a lively forest. Her technique is perfect for this genre of folk rock, and probably the main reason for Gåte's longevity as a band. Adorning the surrounding area of the wreath are class-act musicians wielding an assortment of traditional instruments. Right-hand man Magnus Børmark plays guitar but also the Swedish nyckelharpa, drummer Jon Even Schärer handles all sorts of percussion, as well as a mouth harp, and Arent Todal tackles various stringed instruments. Further adding to the wreath (specifically to Sigil) is the legion of session artists. I may not be able to quickly discern Marit Aspås's cello from Olav Luksengård Mjelva's hardanger fiddle, but these instruments are key in creating the record's environment. Don't expect these instruments to shred at full capacity. Sigil is a slow burner, churning atmospheres with crescendos rather than jamming out. Although the ambiances Gåte builds are splendid, not a single song runs over five minutes long. This hinders what these ten songs could be. The best pieces like "Strandvaskar" pull off heavy-hitting, successful climaxes, while others like "Nokon" spend too much time creating the liftoff for a climax. I adore the slow songs, especially the pairing of ballads ending the album, and now that the band is on a bigger label, a more digestible approach to their wizardry is expected. But if Gåte's mission is to conjure grand images of Nordic myths and legends, packing it all into three-minute chunks probably isn't the right way to go about it. Sigil by Gåte

items.body: 「世界3大ジャズ・フェス」に数えられるスイスのモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバル（Montreux Jazz Festival）。これまで幅広いジャンルのミュージシャンが熱演を繰り広げてきたこのフェスの特徴は、50年を超える歴史を通じてライブ音源と映像が豊富にストックされている点にある。その中からCD、DVD、デジタル音源などでリリースされている「名盤」を紹介していく。 アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム、あるいはダラー・ブランド。アパルトヘイト下の南アフリカでジャズの演奏を始め、その後国外に逃れて音楽活動を続けた名ピアニストが91年の長い人生を終えたのは、今年(2026年)の6月だった。ソロ、デュオ、トリオ、コンボ、オーケストラと、あらゆるフォーマットで作品を残した彼の音楽のエッセンスに触れられるのが、1980年のモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバルの記録『アット・モントルー』である。そのアルバムを紹介しながら、彼のキャリアを偲ぶ。 『アフリカン・ピアノ』の衝撃 ダラー・ブランドがイスラム教に改宗し、名をアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムとしたのは1968年である。彼の代表作として知られる『アフリカン・ピアノ』が、デンマークの首都コペンハーゲンでライブ録音されたのは69年だから、その時点で彼はすでにアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムになっていたことになる。しかし彼は、ダラー・ブランドとしてその後しばらく活動を続けた。 『アフリカン・ピアノ』の名義は、現行盤ではアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムとなっているが、長らくダラー・ブランド名義で流通してきた。ダラー・ブランドという名の方が現在でも通りがいいのは、ひとえに『アフリカン・ピアノ』の圧倒的な知名度による。 もっとも、ダラー・ブランドという名も実は本名ではなく、出生名をアドルフ・ヨハネス・ブランドといった。ダラーとは「ドル」のことで、南アフリカの故郷ケープタウンの港に寄港した水兵にドル札を渡してジャズのSP盤を熱心に収集していたことで、ダラーが彼のニックネームとなったのだった。 名作『アフリカン・ピアノ』の原盤権を当初持っていたのは、デンマークで1969年から72年までの短い期間活動したスペクテイター・レコードだった。73年になってECMのサブ・レーベルであるJAPOからリリースされたことで、このアルバムは広く世界に知られることになった。現在では、この作品はECMを代表するピアノ・ソロ作としての地位を不動のものにしている。アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムのほかのアルバムは聴いたことがなくても、『アフリカン・ピアノ』は何度も聴いたというジャズ・ファンはわが国でも少なくないと思う。 70年代初頭と言えば、モダン・ジャズが雑多な要素を吸収して鵺（ぬえ）のような音楽に変貌しつつあった頃だが、その時代でも『アフリカン・ピアノ』は奇異な作品であったと思う。延々と繰り返される反復フレーズ。スコールのように畳みかける旋律。隙間なく連続し、どこが始まりでどこが終わりか判然としない楽曲──。それは、アメリカのジャズ、あるいはアメリカの黒人音楽とは明らかに異質な音楽だった。 南アが生んだ3人の世界的ミュージシャン 現在聴くことができるアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの最も古い録音は、ジャズ・エピッスルズというセクステットによるもので、レコーディングは1959年であった。このバンドには、やはりのちに世界的なミュージシャンとなるトランペッターのヒュー・マセケラも在籍していた。マセケラが「グレイジング・イン・ザ・グラス」で全米1位を獲得するのは68年のことである。 ジャズ・エピッスルズのメンバーのうち3人は、南ア初の黒人ミュージカル『キング・コング』に参加していて、マセケラもそのひとりだった。『キング・コング』のヒロインとして舞台に立ったのがミリアム・マケバで、彼女もまたのちに世界的シンガーとなる。マセケラとマケバは、わずか2年だが結婚していたこともあった。アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム、ヒュー・マセケラ、ミリアム・マケバ。南アが生んだこの3人のスターが同じコミュニティから出発したのは、南アのジャズ・シーンそのものが小さなコミュニティだったからである。 ジャズ・エピッスルズは、南アで公式に発売された初めての黒人ジャズ・バンドのレコードだった。『ヴァース1』がそのタイトルだったが、『ヴァース2』が録音されることはついになかった。アパルトヘイト下の南アにあって、黒人ならびにその音楽であるジャズに対する弾圧がほどなく激化したことがその理由である。 南ア独自のタウンシップ・ジャズ 1994年まで南アフリカの政権を握ったNP（国民党）が、悪名高い人種分離政策であるアパルトヘイトを掲げたのは1948年だった。南ア人は、「白人」「カラード」「インド人」「アフリカ人」の4つのカテゴリーに分けられ、結婚やセックスによる人種混淆を妨げる法律が整備されて、居住区の分割や都市における人種隔離が進められた。 人種の分類上、ヒュー・マセケラとミリアム・マケバは「アフリカ人」、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムは白人と黒人の混血である「カラード」であった。3人はいずれも1960年代に母国をあとにしたが、その後マセケラとマケバが90年代まで一度も帰国が叶わなかったのに対し、イブラヒムは何度か国に帰ることを許されている。これは、「アフリカ人」と「カラード」の法的権利の違いによるものだったと思われる。 人種分離は、トイレ、レストラン、ホテル、劇場から、バス、学校、役場にまで及び、社会生活のあらゆる領域が「ヨーロッパ人」向けと「非ヨーロッパ人」向けに分けられた。「ヨーロッパ人」とは、南アへの初期入植者であるオランダ人と、その後入植してきたイギリス人を主に指す。 しかし、オランダ人とイギリス人の間にもまた格差はあって、南アの経済、政治、社会の上層を長らく支配してきたのはイギリス人だった。イギリス人支配に対するオランダ人のルサンチマンの結晶のような政党がNPで、その初期の構成員の多くは、戦時にあってナチス・ドイツを支持した者たちだった。政権を握った彼らが設計したアパルトヘイトの諸制度は、しばしばナチスのユダヤ人政策に比して語られる。 アパルトヘイトは、アメリカ南部で1860年代から100年間にわたって存続した人種差別法「ジム・クロウ法」にも似ていたが、それ以上に残酷であったのは、アメリカにはなかった黒人の強制移住があったことによる。 1923年に施行された原住民都市地域法という法律によって、黒人は「タウンシップ」と呼ばれた隔離居住区に住むことを強制された。最も古いタウンシップはイブラヒムの故郷であったケープタウンにあって、その後南ア全土にタウンシップが設けられた。ここで独自に発展したのが、タウンシップ・ジャズである。 アメリカのラグタイムやスウィングと南アの土着の音楽が混じり合って生まれたのがタウンシップ・ジャズで、そこにカリブ海の音楽の要素も感じられるのは、ニューオリンズを経由してもたらされた影響があったからかもしれない。また、南アはある時期までイギリスの旧植民地や入植地の共同体である英連邦の構成国であったから、同じく英連邦の国であったジャマイカやバルバドスから音楽が伝わるルートもおそらくあっただろう。 禁じられたジャズと音楽家たちの出国 1950年代になって、タウンシップ・ジャズと、その後に輸入されたアメリカのジャズをベースにしたジャズ・バンドがいくつか生まれた。ジャズ・エピッスルズがその代表格だったが、彼らが最初のアルバムをレコーディングしてほどなく、南ア史に残る事件が起きた。1960年3月21日の「シャープヴィル虐殺」である。 アパルトヘイト下の南アでは、黒人に身分証の常時携帯を義務づける「パス法」という法律があった。それに抗議するために南アの首都ヨハネスブルグ近郊シャープヴィルの警察署に集まった黒人群衆に警察が発砲した事件が「シャープヴィル虐殺」で、これによって69人が殺され、180人以上が負傷した。 反アパルトヘイト運動のリーダーであり、1962年に逮捕されて以後27年間を獄中で過ごしたのがネルソン・マンデラだった。アパルトヘイト撤廃後の新生南ア初の大統領に就任した彼の歩みを描いた映画『マンデラ 自由への長い道』に、シャープヴィル虐殺の場面が出てくる。犠牲者の多くは、警察の装甲車から逃げ惑う中、背後から無差別に撃たれたのだった。この事件は海外各国に衝撃を与え、国連は3月21日を国際人種差別撤廃デーと定めた。 この事件をきっかけに、南ア全土に抗議行動が広がり、それにともなって南ア政府の弾圧も激化した。ジャズの演奏やラジオでの放送も禁止され、ジャズ・エピッスルズは解散を余儀なくされた。その後、先の3人は故郷を後にすることになる。ヒュー・マセケラがロンドンに活動の場を移したのが1960年、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムが欧州に移住したのが62年で、これはマンデラが逮捕されたのと同じ年であった。ミリアム・マケバは、反アパルトヘイト運動に関与した咎で、67年に国外追放されている。 サックス・プレーヤーとしてのイブラヒム 欧州に活動の場を求めたアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの庇護者となったのが、デューク・エリントンだった。スイスにツアーで訪れていたエリントンにイブラヒムの演奏を聴くよう懇願したのは、彼の婚約者であったと伝わる。 イブラヒムのトリオの演奏を気に入ったエリントンは、この有望なピアニストのワールドワイドのデビュー作となる『デューク・エリントン・プレゼンツ・ザ・ダラー・ブランド・トリオ』のレコーディングを支援した。リリースされたのは、フランク・シナトラが1961年に設立したリプリーズ・レコードからだった。 その後イブラヒムは数々のアルバムをレコーディングすることになるが、最も多くのアルバムを残したのは、ドイツのレーベル、エンヤ（Enja）である。エンヤの設立は1971年で、これはECM設立の翌年に当たる。Enjaというレーベル名は「European New Jazz」の略で、この場合の「New」はアメリカのジャズに対して「新しい」のみならず、ECMよりもさらに「新しい」音楽を目指そうとする意気込みの表現でもあっただろう。 1980年、イブラヒムはモントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバルに出演して8曲を演奏した。うち6曲を収録したライブ盤がリリースされたのも、やはりエンヤからだった。 バンドは、アルト・サックス、トロンボーンをフロントに擁したクインテットだったが、冒頭の「ツァクヴェ」では明らかに3本の管の音が聞こえる。日本盤CDのライナーノーツには「3管を含むセクステットの一体感をアピールしている」という意味不明の記述があるが、3管に聞こえるのはイブラヒムもサックスを吹いているからである。 イブラヒムは、ピアノ以外にフルートやチェロなどを奏する多才な音楽家だった。モントルーではソプラノ・サックスを吹いていて、それがたんなる余技とは言えないのは、6曲中3曲でピアノを弾かずにソプラノを吹いているからだ。裏ジャケットのクレジットも「Soprano Saxophone, Piano」と、サックスが先になっている。 アルバムの最後の曲「イシュマエル」は、ベースの反復フレーズが延々と繰り返されるイブラヒムの代表曲のひとつだが、この曲で彼は堂々たるサックス・ソロを披露していて、吹き終えたのち、客席から大きな喝采を受けている。 イブラヒムの音楽の広大な世界 モントルーのライブ盤はわずか6曲だが、驚くほど多様であったイブラヒムの音楽がこの一枚に凝縮されていると感じる。タウンシップ・ジャズ、サンバ、アラビア音楽、デューク・エリントン、セロニアス・モンク──。これも彼の代表曲である「ザ・ウェディング」は、雑多な原料を混ぜ合わせ、それを蒸留したのちに残った原酒のように澄明で美しい。 アルト・サックスのほかにフルートも吹くカルロス・ワードはパナマ出身のプレーヤーで、ジョン・コルトレーン、ドン・チェリー、セシル・テイラーらとの共演で知られている。イブラヒムとは、ドン・チェリーとのトリオで録音した1972年のライブ盤『第三世界＝アンダーグラウンド／The Third World-Underground』からのつきあいであり、その後デュオ作も一緒にレコーディングしている。 『第三世界＝アンダーグラウンド』は何度も繰り返し聴きたくなる名作である。チェリーの個性が大いに発揮されているが、とくにアヴァンギャルドな作品ではない。このアルバムと、ソロ作の『アフリカン・ピアノ』、さらにオーケストラと共演した何枚かの作品のうちのひとつ、例えば『アフリカ組曲／African Suite』などをこのモントルーのライブ盤と合わせて聴けば、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの広大な世界の概要を知ることができると思う。エンヤにレコーディングされたアルバムから10曲をセレクトした『プレミアム・ベスト』というCDもまた、格好の手引きとなるだろう。 2011年のモアーズ・フェスティバルにて 独唱によって閉じられた長いキャリア 2024年、アブドゥーラ・イブラヒムはロンドンのバービカン・センターでコンサートを行い、その演奏をレコーディングした。フルート奏者と、ベース／チェロ奏者とのトリオによるライブで、そのアルバムに『3』というタイトルがつけられたのは、トリオ演奏であるからだけではなく、アルバムが3部構成になっているからである。 1部には、ライブ前の無観客のホールで、8トラックのアナログ・テープ・マシンで録音した6曲が収録されている。資料によれば、この機材はエルヴィス・プレスリーがデビュー曲「イッツ・オール・ライト」を録音した際に使ったものであり、メンフィスのサン・スタジオにあったその機材を現在所有しているのは、ブラーのデーモン・アルバーンだそうである。そのテープ・マシンを、デーモンのスタジオからバービカン・センターに運んで録音が行われたのだった。 2部、3部は客を入れたのちのライブ演奏で、2部ではイブラヒムのヒーローであったエリントンの「イン・ア・センチメンタル・ムード」と、ジョン・コルトレーンの「ジャイアント・ステップス」、3部ではセロニアス・モンクの「スキッピー」を演奏している。 2部と3部には「リプライズ」と題されたピアノ・ソロの演奏が収められているが、注意深く耳を傾ければ、その中にジャズ・エピッスルズの名曲「ブルース・フォー・ヒューイ」のメロディを聴くことができる。「ヒューイ」はヒュー・マセケラの愛称である。南アのジャズの歴史をともにつくった古い友に対する変わらぬ友情をイブラヒムは示そうとしたのかもしれない。マセケラの死去から6年が経っていた。 2回目のアンコールで、イブラヒムはアカペラで歌を歌っている。アフリカの民族語と英語をまじえて歌われるその歌には、「伝達──幾世紀の歴史をもつ海運貨物の音」というタイトルがつけられている。何世紀にもわたって海運で運ばれていった貨物。それが何を意味するか、言うまでもあるまい。 このアルバムが、結果的にアブドゥーラ・イブラヒムの遺作となった。アフリカの奴隷貿易の歴史を歌う独唱で、イブラヒムは長いキャリアを閉じた。彼の新作がもはや聴けなくなった今、残された膨大な作品の森にあらためて分け入りたく思う。 文／二階堂 尚 『At Montreux』 アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム／ダラー・ブランド ■1.Tsakve 2. Whoza Mtwana 3. The Homecoming Song 4. The Wedding 5. The Perfumed Forest Wet With Rain 6. Ismael ■アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム(ss,p)、カルロス・ワード(as,fl)、クレイグ・ハリス(tb)、アロンゾ・ガードナー(b)、アンドレ・ストロパート(ds) ■第14回モントルー・ジャズ・フェスティバル／1980年7月18日   投稿 【アブドゥーラ・イブラヒム】長い歩みを終えた南アフリカの名ピアニスト ─ライブ盤で聴くモントルー Vol.69 は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.album: Charlie May / Trusted Farms (ASIPV058)
items.body:
After decades contributing to records where a single riff could transform a dancefloor, Charlie May turns that instinct inward on Trusted Farms. 

 For over thirty years, Charlie has occupied a position that seems increasingly rare in electronic music: the musician’s musician, the person behind the machines, the extra pair of hands in the studio, and quite often, the person responsible for the melody you end up carrying around in your head for weeks on end. 

 Alongside Duncan Forbes as Spooky, Charlie helped shape some of the most important electronic music to emerge from the UK in the early ’90s. That partnership would also sow the seeds for one of Sasha’s defining records: the central riff behind Xpander began life in Spooky’s live material, before Charlie brought the idea into the studio with Sasha and helped transform it into one of electronic music’s most enduring anthems.

 astrangelyisolatedplace · ASIPV058 Charlie May / Trusted Farms [PREVIEWS] 

 Listen closely to Charlie’s work and there’s a particular instinct that keeps returning: knowing when a simple synth line is enough. Knowing which note needs to change. Knowing when repetition stops being repetition and starts becoming the entire reason a track works. More recently, as one-third of Quiet Places on ASIP, he’s taken those same instincts somewhere looser — beatless, gridless and led by improvisation.

 Trusted Farms puts those instincts front and centre.

 Tiny melodic phrases appear and refuse to leave. Synth lines repeat just long enough to become lodged in your head. Parts rub against each other without being tidied into submission. There’s a sharpness and directness to it all amongst the purposeful analogue warmth.

 Some of these tracks feel almost ridiculously simple at first. But simplicity is difficult when you’ve spent decades learning every possible way to complicate something. Many of the parts on Trusted Farms were performed live with minimal editing. A synth line might be doubled, distorted, re-recorded and pushed back through another piece of equipment, but it remains the same idea. Instead of filling the gaps, Charlie works on the weight and character of what is already there. The melodies become physical; slightly worn around the edges.

 For someone whose fingerprints can be found across some genuinely monumental moments in electronic music, Charlie has spent decades knowing what to add. Trusted Farms is about knowing exactly what to leave alone.

 Available on black 12” and digital, mastered by Andreas Lupo LOOP-O Lubich and featuring artwork by Peter Skwiot Smith, Trusted Farms will be available on October 16th 2026.

items.body: Everybody Else’s Life, Too is the latest from Josh Berman, a stalwart of the Chicago scene still somewhat underappreciated outside of his hometown. He has played the gamut of Chicago improvisors (including Mars Williams’ A Very Ayler Xmas project, the all-too-short-lived Michael Zerrang and the Blue Lights, and Ken Vandermark’s Audio One), sneaked across the Atlantic to record with Paul Lytton, Edward Perraud, and Jon Rune Strøm, and led several of his own bands. On this one, he is joined by bassist Jason Roebke – a reliably punchy oft-times sideman of Chicago circles - and the indefatigable drummer Chris Corsano for a live date at Chicago’s Constellation from 2025. I cannot say there is much surprising here if you are familiar with Berman’s previous headline albums. That said, this is more of what this listener wants rather than simply more of the same. Berman clearly has a thing for bop, in its various forms, and maybe the title is even a nod to his appreciation of those who came before and inspired him. The songs on here start with a catchy head, or a few more plodding, smokey ones, and from there break down into spurs, knotty angles, and spindly striations. One could play this album for someone who thought Miles went too far when he went electric, or Coltrane with Ascension, and they would happily bob their head along with Roebke’s walking bass or Corsano’s steady patter behind Berman’s jumpy melodies. But restricting this to such a palatable bridge would miss the other point, which lies in the free form sections that, yes, are tied to the head but in a sensual way that deviates from its rhythm, tune, and key in favor of capturing, extending, and straining the intricacies of a spontaneous moment. Those sections are when Berman stretches into flutters, crackles, and bites, when Roebke leans into timbre, and Corsano eschews rhythm for sound. Those sections are limited; in this case I think for the better. That is not because trio cannot stretch out into the unknown. (Take the eighth cut, Scale, as an example of their exploratory chops.) Instead, it is because they do so within Berman’s bookending melodic confines that set the direction and mark the terminal point. And were those themes not inspired, this would fall flat. But they are and do not. For doubters, just listen to the wonderfully lonesome and wistful closer, Second Look, where Corsano’s brushes lay a soft-rain backdrop to Berman’s and Roebke’s melancholic dialog. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is much in the vein of a different Josh Berman Trio’s A Dance and a Hop (2015) and should be considered an expansion of that project. Again, you might well know what to expect if you have been following Berman already, but that does not make what you hear any less satisfying. Everybody Else’s Life, Too is available download from Bandcamp and a CD from a few choice independent music outlets. See the CvD website for more . Everybody Else's Life, Too by Josh Berman Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: ACT, 2026 Personnel - Emile Parisien: soprano saxophone; Yaron Herman: piano; Linda May Han Oh: bass; Prabhu Edouard: tabla, percussion, voice. French soprano saxophonist and composer Emile Parisien is an eclectic jazz practitioner with inestimable musical gifts that allow him to explore a whole universe of sound. Parisien brings a glowing selection of tunes composed by himself, pianist and longtime collaborator Yaron Herman, and proficient bassist Linda May Han Oh, alongside two covers. Rounding out the quartet is tabla player and vocalist Prabhu Edouard, who helps establish an organically integrated framework for the leader’s world-fusion aesthetics. This group was formed after a memorable first performance in Paris. Floating opens with Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff and Thomas de Hartmann’s “ Asian Songs & Rhythms, No. 40 ”, a peaceful, spiritual tune that, combining Eastern modal traditions with Western classical sensibilities, slowly unfolds with a ternary feel. Parisien employs his intervallic expertise in vibrant phrasing, while Herman evokes distant, serene landscapes. The other cover on the album is Anouar Brahem’s “ Badhra ”—the fantastic opening track of his trio album Thimar—which scintillates with sophistication and enchantment. In the latter, Herman’s clarity of speech and objectivity pair well with the in-and-out lyricism of Parisien, while the duo’s co-written piece, “ Portal ”, keeps the rhythmic momentum going after a dynamic introduction centered on Edouard, who doubles on tabla and voice. Herman’ piano solo on this one is pure delight. On the other hand, Parisien’s “ Bonbon ” is filled with excitement and aligned with Middle Eastern traditions. Herman contributes five compositions of his own: the waltzing ballads “ Olive Branch ” and “ Ruth ”, with the latter acquiring a jazzier, Keith Jarrett-esque vibe before morphing into a more percussive passage over which Parisien’s soprano glides effortlessly; the playful and bluesy “ Nusrat ”; and the stop-and-go flow of “ El Toro ”, a showcase for Oh’s rhythmic adroitness. Sandwiched between the latter two tracks is the bassist’s “ As It Comes And As It Goes ”, a moment of reflection and an opportunity to hear her unaccompanied. According to the bandleader, this is music about peace, poetry, and love, and listeners should be able to feel its emotional appeal as well as the group’s ability to communicate through whatever musical language they choose to mix in. This forward-looking diversity is key, and Parisien’s fusion is not without an airily contemporary touch. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Asian Songs & Rhythms, No 40 ► 04 - Badhra ► 08 - Nusrat

items.body:
SB19's music made its way onto the international dance stage as Jam Republic SEA took a Round 1 win over Auckland’s Royal Family on 20 September at the International Dance League Championship 2026 in Los Angeles.

Representing Southeast Asia, Jam Republic SEA brought the P-pop supergroup along for the ride, with SB19 tracks 'GENTO' and 'DAM' featuring in the crew’s incredible routine.

The Championship, held at the Shrine Expo Hall, marked the finale of the International Dance League’s inaugural season. The competition brought together six professional teams across five Series in New York, Vancouver, Sydney, Seoul, and Los Angeles, with points earned throughout the season determining the matchups for the Championship.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Jam Republic SEA entered the Championship as the fifth seed, setting up a Round 1 head-to-head against second-seeded Royal Family. Under the Championship format, the first round paired the first and sixth seeds, second and fifth seeds, and third and fourth seeds, with each winner advancing to the final round.

Flying the flag for Southeast Asia, Jam Republic SEA’s current IDL roster includes dancers from the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, Indonesia, and beyond. The team is part of Singapore-founded dance agency Jam Republic, which IDL announced for the season with a 25-dancer roster drawn from 10 countries.

With 'GENTO' and 'DAM' in the mix, Jam Republic SEA turned their Round 1 win into a full-on Southeast Asian moment on the global stage.

items.body:
Fans of rookie K-pop girl group UNCHILD are calling on HIGH UP Entertainment for answers following weeks of uncertainty surrounding the group’s activities and future.

The six-member act debuted earlier this year and includes Na Haeun, who was already known among K-pop fans as a child dancer before joining the group.

Concern surrounding UNCHILD grew after the group’s planned comeback was postponed indefinitely. With few subsequent updates, fans began rallying around the hashtag #WhereIsUNCHILD, asking HIGH UP Entertainment to clarify the members’ status and the group’s future.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

The situation drew further attention on 21 September, when an anonymous message posted on Korean platform Spin and subsequently shared on X claimed to have been written by someone working in the entertainment industry.

The anonymous post alleged that an investor had withdrawn funding from HIGH UP Entertainment following a negative reaction to UNCHILD’s upcoming material. It further claimed that the company was experiencing financial difficulties, had laid off staff, and was no longer able to properly manage the group.

The writer also suggested that UNCHILD could be preparing to disband.

None of these claims have been independently verified, and HIGH UP Entertainment has not announced UNCHILD’s disbandment.

The X post sharing the allegations had amassed more than 1.9 million views. With speculation continuing to circulate online, fans are calling for an official statement from HIGH UP Entertainment addressing UNCHILD’s current status and future activities.

items.body:
proya Plays With Ambient Music's Capacity To Comfort & Be Discomforting On EP 'Subliminal'

21 September 2026

Infusing a narrative in an ambient work, a genre often more about calm than movement by its initial design, is not a common achievement by budding artists of the genre. Therefore, it's remarkable to see Mumbai's Priya Panchwadkar aka proya manage it on her debut EP 'Subliminal'.

The wall of sound on 'find me', both placating and abrasive, echoes alongside the titular line, gradually unwinding into a tangible melodic run – something palpable finally being found from the dense cloud of sound. The metallic palette of 'INT' shifts into more botanica textures where the machine-like hiss feels more like rain before entering a more discomfortably strobing space. One shift too many for our taste, where perhaps sonic experimentation overtook compositional control, but undoubtedly creating an impressive musical world in each of its segments.

The EP title doesn't mislead, and while there are low hums that create a sense of liminal space, like on 'harvest/arriving', the producer and lens-based artist enchants the metaphorical air in those metaphorical spaces with a mix of held chords and their atonal distortions to speak more to emotions than memory of something outward. For every pleasant chime and horn line on 'snow', there is the harsh hiss and rattle of 'UGH'.

Check out the EP 'Subliminal' below and follow proya for more information.

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
